items.gloss_md: Five-parameter score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy; 5–15 points) that grades the severity of cirrhosis as class A (5–6), B (7–9) or C (10–15).
items.body_md:
| Parameter | 1 point | 2 points | 3 points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bilirubin (mg/dL) | <2 | 2–3 | >3 |
| Albumin (g/dL) | >3.5 | 2.8–3.5 | <2.8 |
| INR | <1.7 | 1.7–2.3 | >2.3 |
| Ascites | none | mild/controlled | moderate–severe |
| Encephalopathy | none | grade 1–2 | grade 3–4 |

Bilirubin in µmol/L: <34, 34–50, >50. For PBC/PSC, higher bilirubin cut-offs are used (1–4, 4–10, >10 mg/dL).

- Class A = 5–6, B = 7–9, C = 10–15. One-year survival is roughly 100%, 80% and 45% (classical figures).
- Uses: prognosis, surgical risk, eligibility for resection, TACE and systemic HCC therapy (most trials: Child A), drug dosing (labels state Child-Pugh classes), pre-emptive TIPS (C 10–13).
- Weaknesses: two subjective parameters (ascites, HE), ceiling effects, no renal function. For allocation, MELD replaced it.

attrs.mnemonic: 'ABCDE': Albumin, Bilirubin, Coagulation (INR), Distension (ascites), Encephalopathy. Classes: 5–6 A, 7–9 B, 10–15 C.
attrs.anecdote: Charles Gardner Child and Jeremiah Turcotte proposed the original score in 1964 to predict mortality after portocaval shunt surgery. It included nutritional status. R. N. H. Pugh and colleagues replaced nutrition with prothrombin time in 1973 for patients undergoing oesophageal transection for bleeding varices.

items.gloss_md: End stage of chronic liver fibrosis, in which bridging fibrous septa surround regenerative nodules, destroying the normal architecture. It leads to portal hypertension, loss of liver function and a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.body_md:
- Causes in Germany and Europe: mainly alcohol and MASLD (rising), then chronic hepatitis B/C, autoimmune and cholestatic diseases (AIH, PBC, PSC), haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, A1AT deficiency, and cardiac congestion. Cryptogenic cirrhosis is often 'burnt-out' MASH.
- Histology: METAVIR F4 / Ishak 5–6. Macronodular, micronodular or mixed.
- Clinical course: compensated (often asymptomatic, median survival over 12 years) progresses to decompensated (ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, jaundice; median survival about 2 years).
- Diagnosis: imaging, elastography (≥15 kPa highly suggestive of cACLD), laboratory signs (low platelets, high INR and bilirubin, low albumin), biopsy if needed.
- Management: treat the cause, carry out HCC surveillance (ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months), screen for varices or start carvedilol, give vaccinations and nutrition. Prognosis is graded with Child-Pugh and MELD. Liver transplantation is the definitive therapy.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) The 'Schrumpfleber' (shrunken liver): nodular, hard and small. Greek kirrhos = tawny/yellow-orange, the colour Laennec saw.
attrs.anecdote: René Laennec, inventor of the stethoscope, coined the term 'cirrhosis' in 1819 from the Greek 'kirrhos' (yellowish-orange) for the colour of the nodular livers he saw at autopsy. Alcoholic cirrhosis was long called 'Laennec cirrhosis'.

items.label_md: Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score
items.gloss_md: Objective score from bilirubin, INR and creatinine (range 6–40) that predicts 3-month mortality in chronic liver disease. It is the basis of liver allocation in Eurotransplant and the US.
items.body_md:
MELD = 3.78 × ln(bilirubin, mg/dL) + 11.2 × ln(INR) + 9.57 × ln(creatinine, mg/dL) + 6.43 (equivalently 10 × [0.957 × ln creatinine + 0.378 × ln bilirubin + 1.120 × ln INR + 0.643], the UNOS form).

- Values below 1 are set to 1. Creatinine is capped at 4 mg/dL (set to 4 with dialysis twice in the past week). The result is rounded and bounded 6–40.
- 3-month mortality rises steeply: a MELD below 10 corresponds to a few percent, 20–29 to about 20%, 30–39 to about 50%, and 40 or more to over 70% (classic figures).
- 'Lab MELD' is calculated from labs. 'Match MELD' is used for allocation and includes exception points (e.g. HCC within Milan, HPS, PSC with recurrent cholangitis).
- Eurotransplant introduced MELD-based allocation in Germany in December 2006.
- Limitations: does not capture sodium, sarcopenia or complications such as refractory ascites or HE; women are disadvantaged by creatinine. This led to MELD-Na and MELD 3.0.

attrs.mnemonic: MELD needs 'BIC': Bilirubin, INR, Creatinine. Range 6–40. 'Above 15 the transplant helps more than it hurts' (the survival-benefit threshold usually cited).
attrs.anecdote: MELD was developed at the Mayo Clinic (Malinchoc et al., 2000) to predict survival after elective TIPS placement, not for transplant allocation. It proved so good at predicting 3-month mortality that UNOS adopted it for liver allocation in 2002.

items.gloss_md: Macrolide calcineurin inhibitor (FK506) that binds FKBP12 and blocks T-cell activation. It is the most widely used maintenance immunosuppressant after kidney and liver transplantation and is dosed by whole-blood trough levels.
items.body_md:
- Isolated from Streptomyces tsukubaensis in Japan (Fujisawa) in 1984. Clinical use after liver transplantation established by Starzl's group in Pittsburgh from 1989; approved 1994 (US). More potent than ciclosporin with less rejection (Elite-Symphony trial 2007: low-dose tacrolimus regimen best).
- Formulations: twice daily (Prograf and generics), once daily prolonged release (Advagraf), LCP-tacrolimus (Envarsus). Switching formulations requires level checks.
- Monitoring: trough levels (C0, LC-MS/MS or immunoassay). Targets are centre- and time-specific, higher in the first months and lower later. High intra-patient variability (CV) predicts rejection and DSA.
- Metabolism: CYP3A4/3A5. CYP3A5 expressers (*1 carriers) need higher doses. Inhibitors (azoles, clarithromycin, diltiazem, grapefruit, ritonavir/paxlovid) raise levels. Inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) lower them.
- Side effects: nephrotoxicity, tremor and headache, PRES, PTDM (more than ciclosporin), hypertension, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, alopecia, diarrhoea, infections, cancer.
- Topical tacrolimus is used for atopic dermatitis.

attrs.mnemonic: Tacrolimus' three big victims 'K-N-G': Kidney (nephrotoxicity), Nerves (tremor, PRES), Glucose (PTDM).
attrs.anecdote: FK506 was found in a soil sample from near Mount Tsukuba in Japan; its name tacrolimus is coined from 'Tsukuba macrolide immunosuppressant'. Starzl's Pittsburgh team rescued liver recipients with intractable rejection with it in 1989.

items.gloss_md: Immune-mediated injury of a transplanted organ by the recipient's alloreactive T cells and/or antibodies. By timing and mechanism it is classified as hyperacute, acute (T-cell mediated or antibody-mediated) or chronic.
items.body_md:
- Hyperacute: minutes to hours, from preformed antibodies (ABO, HLA). Now very rare thanks to crossmatching.
- Acute T-cell mediated rejection (TCMR): mostly in the first months. Interstitial/tubular or portal inflammation, endotheliitis. Usually responds to steroid pulses.
- Antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR): DSA, microvascular inflammation, C4d. Can be early (preformed DSA) or late (de novo DSA, often from non-adherence). Harder to treat.
- Chronic rejection: progressive graft damage. Kidney: chronic active ABMR with transplant glomerulopathy. Liver: ductopenic rejection. Heart: cardiac allograft vasculopathy. Lung: CLAD.
- Diagnosis: graft biopsy with standardised grading (Banff for kidney, liver, pancreas, heart AMR; ISHLT for heart/lung), DSA testing, increasingly biomarkers (dd-cfDNA, molecular microscope).
- Organ immunogenicity: lung and intestine highest, liver lowest.

attrs.mnemonic: Timeline 'minutes – months – years': hyperacute (antibodies already there), acute (T cells and new antibodies), chronic (slow scarring).
attrs.anecdote: Peter Medawar's skin-graft experiments during and after the Second World War showed that rejection is an immune response with memory ('second-set rejection'). Later work on acquired tolerance earned him the 1960 Nobel Prize with Macfarlane Burnet.

items.label_md: Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system
items.gloss_md: The standard HCC staging system. It combines tumour burden, liver function and performance status into stages 0, A, B, C and D, each linked to a recommended treatment (2022 update).
items.body_md:
- BCLC 0 (very early): single nodule ≤2 cm, preserved liver function, ECOG PS 0. Treatment: ablation; resection (or transplant if not suitable).
- BCLC A (early): single nodule of any size, or 2–3 nodules each ≤3 cm, preserved function, PS 0. Treatment: resection, liver transplantation, ablation.
- BCLC B (intermediate): multinodular, preserved function, PS 0. Treatment: transplantation (extended criteria), TACE, or systemic therapy (diffuse, infiltrative or extensive bilobar disease).
- BCLC C (advanced): portal invasion and/or extrahepatic spread, preserved function, PS 1–2. Treatment: systemic therapy.
- BCLC D (terminal): end-stage liver function (not a transplant candidate) and/or PS 3–4. Best supportive care.

The 2022 update (Reig et al., J Hepatol) uses ALBI and AFP, the concept of 'treatment stage migration' (offering the next stage's therapy when the stage-matched one is unsuitable), and lists atezolizumab-bevacizumab and durvalumab-tremelimumab as first-line systemic therapy.

attrs.mnemonic: 0-A-B-C-D maps to 'Ablate – Area/Ablate/Allograft (resect, transplant) – Block the artery (TACE) – Chemicals (systemic) – Don't (best supportive care)'.
attrs.anecdote: Developed by Josep M. Llovet, Jordi Bruix and colleagues at the Hospital Clínic in Barcelona, first published in 1999. Llovet also led the SHARP trial that made sorafenib the first effective systemic HCC drug in 2008.

items.gloss_md: Primary liver cancer arising from hepatocytes, usually in cirrhosis or chronic HBV. It is the most common primary liver malignancy and a leading cause of cancer death worldwide.
items.body_md:
- Risk factors: cirrhosis of any cause (annual incidence about 1–8%), chronic HBV (even without cirrhosis), HCV, alcohol, MASLD (HCC also without cirrhosis), aflatoxin, haemochromatosis.
- Molecular hallmarks: TERT promoter mutations (most common, about 60%), CTNNB1 (β-catenin) and TP53 mutations, AXIN1, ARID1A. HBV integration. Few actionable driver alterations.
- Diagnosis: in high-risk patients non-invasively by multiphase CT/MRI (arterial hyperenhancement + washout, LI-RADS 5). Biopsy if atypical. AFP is supportive and prognostic.
- Staging and treatment by BCLC. Curative options: resection, ablation, transplantation (Milan). Locoregional: TACE, SIRT. Systemic: atezolizumab + bevacizumab, durvalumab + tremelimumab, nivolumab + ipilimumab, or TKIs (sorafenib, lenvatinib).
- Surveillance of cirrhotic patients: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months.

attrs.mnemonic: HCC lives on the artery: it 'lights up early and washes out late' on imaging, and arterial therapies (TACE, SIRT) target that supply.

items.gloss_md: Replacement of a diseased liver with a whole or partial graft from a deceased or living donor. It is the only curative treatment for end-stage liver disease, acute liver failure and selected liver tumours, with about 90% one-year and 70–75% five-year patient survival.
items.body_md:
- Indications: decompensated cirrhosis (alcohol, MASH, viral, PBC, PSC, AIH); HCC within criteria (Milan); acute liver failure; metabolic disorders (Wilson, A1AT, familial amyloidosis, urea cycle defects); paediatric biliary atresia.
- Listing usually considered from MELD ≥15 or at first decompensation.
- Technique: orthotopic, either replacing the IVC or with piggyback (cava-preserving) technique. Anastomoses: hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic veins/cava, bile duct (duct-to-duct or hepaticojejunostomy).
- Graft types: whole liver (DBD), split liver, living-donor lobe, DCD (not in Germany).
- Early complications: PNF, EAD, hepatic artery thrombosis, bleeding, biliary leaks/strictures, acute rejection, infection. Late: CNI nephrotoxicity, metabolic syndrome, de novo cancers, disease recurrence, chronic rejection (rare).
- In Germany about 750–850 liver transplants per year in about 20 centres.

attrs.anecdote: Thomas Starzl performed the first human liver transplant in Denver in 1963 (the patient, a 3-year-old boy, died during surgery). The first long-term success followed in 1967. Starzl's results only became good after the introduction of ciclosporin in the early 1980s.

items.gloss_md: Hepatic steatosis together with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor and no other cause of steatosis. It is the 2023 name for what was called NAFLD and the most common chronic liver disease worldwide.
items.body_md:
- Definition (2023 multisociety Delphi consensus): steatosis (imaging or histology) + ≥1 of 5 cardiometabolic criteria: (1) BMI ≥25 kg/m² (≥23 in Asians) or waist above 94 cm (men) / 80 cm (women); (2) fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), or 2-h glucose ≥140 mg/dL, or HbA1c ≥5.7%, or type 2 diabetes or its treatment; (3) blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg or treatment; (4) triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL (1.70 mmol/L) or treatment; (5) HDL ≤40 mg/dL (men) / ≤50 mg/dL (women) or treatment.
- Alcohol intake below 20 g/day (women) or 30 g/day (men). Above that, the disease is MetALD or alcohol-associated liver disease.
- Prevalence about 30% of adults worldwide, much higher in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
- Spectrum: steatosis (MASL), steatohepatitis (MASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC (HCC can also arise without cirrhosis).
- Genetics: PNPLA3 I148M and TM6SF2 E167K increase risk; HSD17B13 loss-of-function variants protect.
- The leading cause of death is cardiovascular disease, followed by extrahepatic cancers and liver disease. Fibrosis stage determines liver outcome.
- Work-up: FIB-4 first, then elastography or ELF (two-step algorithm).

attrs.mnemonic: MASLD = 'Metabolic' replaces 'Non-alcoholic': the name now says what the disease IS (metabolic) rather than what it is not (not alcohol). Five risk factors = the 5 components of metabolic syndrome (BMI/waist, glucose, BP, TG, HDL).
attrs.anecdote: The 2023 renaming was the result of a Delphi process with over 200 experts from many countries, partly because patients found 'non-alcoholic' and 'fatty' stigmatising.

items.gloss_md: The human major histocompatibility complex on chromosome 6p21.3. It encodes the highly polymorphic cell-surface molecules (class I: HLA-A, -B, -C; class II: HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) that present peptides to T cells and are the main targets of the immune response against transplants.
items.body_md:
- Class I (all nucleated cells) presents peptides to CD8⁺ T cells. Class II (antigen-presenting cells, activated endothelium) presents to CD4⁺ T cells.
- The most polymorphic genes in the human genome, with tens of thousands of known alleles. Inherited as haplotypes, so siblings have a 25% chance of being HLA-identical.
- Nomenclature: HLA-A*02:01:01:01. Field 1 = allele group (approximating the serological antigen, e.g. A2), field 2 = specific protein, further fields = synonymous and non-coding variation. Older serological 'split' names (e.g. B51/B52 from B5) still appear in allocation.
- Transplant relevance: HLA mismatches drive T-cell alloreactivity and formation of anti-HLA antibodies (DSA). Kidney allocation matches HLA-A, -B, -DR. Sensitisation through pregnancy, transfusion or previous transplants limits access to compatible organs.
- Also central in HSCT (10/10 or 12/12 matching), disease association (HLA-B27, HLA-DQ2/8) and drug hypersensitivity (HLA-B*57:01).

attrs.mnemonic: 'ABC are class I, D is class II': A, B, C on every cell, the 'D' genes (DR, DQ, DP) on the immune cells.
attrs.anecdote: Jean Dausset described the first human leukocyte antigen ('MAC', now HLA-A2) in 1958 from antibodies in the sera of multiply transfused patients. He shared the 1980 Nobel Prize with Baruj Benacerraf and George Snell for work on the MHC.

items.gloss_md: Drug therapy that prevents and treats rejection. It consists of induction (intense, peri-operative: basiliximab or depleting antibodies), lifelong maintenance (typically tacrolimus + mycophenolate ± steroids), and treatment of rejection episodes.
items.body_md:
- Standard triple maintenance therapy after kidney transplantation: tacrolimus (CNI) + mycophenolate (antiproliferative) + prednisolone (often tapered or withdrawn). After liver transplantation, lower intensity is common (tacrolimus ± MMF, early steroid withdrawal) because the liver is tolerogenic.
- Intensity is highest in the first 3–6 months and then reduced. It is individualised by immunological risk (sensitisation, DSA, re-transplant), organ, kidney function, infections and cancer.
- Alternatives: mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, sirolimus) for CNI minimisation, cancer or CMV; belatacept (costimulation blockade) for CNI avoidance in kidney recipients.
- Trade-off: too little leads to rejection and DSA; too much leads to infections (CMV, BK, PJP), cancers (skin, PTLD) and drug toxicities (nephrotoxicity, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia).
- Requires therapeutic drug monitoring and attention to drug interactions (CYP3A4).

attrs.mnemonic: Triple therapy = 'T-M-P': Tacrolimus, Mycophenolate, Prednisolone — blocks signal 1 (TCR → calcineurin), proliferation (purines) and inflammation (genes).

items.gloss_md: Transplantation of a kidney from a deceased or living donor into a patient with end-stage kidney disease. It is the most common organ transplant and gives better survival and quality of life than dialysis.
items.body_md:
- Heterotopic placement in the iliac fossa. The native kidneys usually stay. Vascular anastomoses to the iliac vessels, ureter to the bladder (with a temporary stent).
- Pre-emptive transplantation (before dialysis), especially from living donors, gives the best results.
- Living donation makes up about a quarter to a third of kidney transplants in Germany. The deceased-donor waiting time in Germany is often 8 years or more.
- Allocation in Eurotransplant: ETKAS (HLA match, waiting time, sensitisation) and ESP (old-for-old).
- Key issues: HLA matching and crossmatch, sensitisation (PRA/DSA), delayed graft function, rejection (TCMR, ABMR; Banff classification), CNI nephrotoxicity, BK polyomavirus nephropathy, CMV, recurrence of glomerulonephritis (e.g. FSGS, IgA nephropathy).
- Median graft survival is roughly 10–15 years for deceased donors and longer for living donors.

attrs.mnemonic: New kidney goes 'downstairs' (iliac fossa); the old ones usually stay home.

items.gloss_md: Excess accumulation of extracellular matrix (scar, mainly collagen I and III) in the liver as a wound-healing response to chronic injury. Fibrosis stage is the strongest predictor of liver-related outcomes.
items.body_md:
- Pathophysiology: chronic hepatocyte injury (from alcohol, metabolic, viral, autoimmune or cholestatic causes) leads to inflammation and Kupffer-cell/macrophage signals (TGF-β, PDGF). Hepatic stellate cells activate into myofibroblasts and deposit matrix, while TIMPs inhibit its degradation.
- Staging: F0 (none) to F4 (cirrhosis) in METAVIR and NASH CRN; Ishak 0–6. 'Significant' fibrosis means F≥2, 'advanced' F≥3.
- Non-invasive assessment: FIB-4, ELF, transient elastography (kPa), MR elastography.
- Fibrosis is reversible to a substantial degree when the cause is removed (for example after HCV cure, abstinence or weight loss). Advanced cirrhosis with thick septa regresses less.
- In MASLD, fibrosis stage (not NAS activity) predicts mortality. Fibrosis improvement of at least one stage is an accepted surrogate endpoint for conditional drug approval.

attrs.mnemonic: F0 to F4 like school grades in reverse: F4 is the worst, and F4 means cirrhosis. 'Significant' starts at F2, 'advanced' at F3.

items.gloss_md: Replacement of a failing organ (kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas, intestine) with a graft from a deceased or living donor. It requires immunological matching, lifelong immunosuppression and management of rejection, infection and malignancy.
items.body_md:
- Key steps: evaluation and listing, allocation (Eurotransplant), procurement and preservation (cold storage, machine perfusion), implantation, induction and maintenance immunosuppression, monitoring (drug levels, graft function, DSA, biopsies) and management of long-term complications (CNI nephrotoxicity, PTDM, cardiovascular disease, infections, cancer).
- Rejection risk differs by organ. The liver is relatively tolerogenic, while lung and intestine are the most immunogenic.
- Germany has about 3500–4000 organ transplants per year, but more than 8000 people on waiting lists, and one of the lowest deceased donor rates in Europe (about 11 per million inhabitants).
- Typical one-year graft survival is above 90% for kidney and liver.

attrs.mnemonic: The transplant cycle 'L-A-P-I-I-M': Listing, Allocation, Preservation, Implantation, Immunosuppression, Monitoring.
attrs.anecdote: Joseph Murray performed the first successful kidney transplant between identical twins (Richard and Ronald Herrick) in Boston in 1954. Using an identical twin sidestepped rejection. Murray received the 1990 Nobel Prize together with E. Donnall Thomas (bone marrow transplantation).

items.gloss_md: Raised pressure in the portal venous system, usually from cirrhotic intrahepatic resistance plus increased splanchnic inflow. It causes varices, ascites, splenomegaly and hepatic encephalopathy via portosystemic shunts.
items.body_md:
- Measured as HVPG: normal 1–5 mmHg; portal hypertension above 5 mmHg; clinically significant (CSPH) ≥10 mmHg (risk of varices and decompensation); ≥12 mmHg risk of variceal bleeding; ≥20 mmHg in acute bleeding predicts treatment failure.
- Classification by site: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (presinusoidal, e.g. schistosomiasis or early PBC; sinusoidal, i.e. cirrhosis; postsinusoidal, e.g. sinusoidal obstruction syndrome), posthepatic (Budd–Chiari, right heart failure).
- Mechanism in cirrhosis: structural fibrosis plus dynamic vasoconstriction (low intrahepatic NO), then splanchnic vasodilation and a hyperdynamic circulation that further increases portal inflow.
- Consequences: oesophageal/gastric varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, ascites, splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia, HE, hepatorenal syndrome.
- Treatment: non-selective beta-blockers (carvedilol), band ligation, TIPS, and treating the cause.

attrs.mnemonic: HVPG thresholds 5–10–12–20: above 5 'hypertension', 10 'significant' (varices, decompensation), 12 'they bleed', 20 'treatment failure'.

items.gloss_md: Simple non-invasive fibrosis score from age, AST, ALT and platelet count. It is the recommended first-line test to rule out advanced fibrosis in MASLD and other chronic liver diseases.
items.body_md:
FIB-4 = (age [years] × AST [U/L]) / (platelets [10⁹/L] × √ALT [U/L]).

- Below 1.30: low risk of advanced fibrosis (high negative predictive value, above 90%). Above 2.67: high risk, so refer to hepatology. In between: indeterminate, so do a second-line test (transient elastography or ELF).
- For people aged 65 or over, a lower cut-off of 2.0 is recommended (age inflates the score). It is unreliable below about 35 years.
- Developed by Sterling et al. (2006) in HIV/HCV coinfection, later validated in NAFLD and HCV.
- Recommended in the EASL-EASD-EASO 2024 and AASLD guidance as step 1 of the two-step MASLD pathway in primary care and diabetology.
- Easy to compute from routine EHR data, so it is popular in registry and real-world studies.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Age and AST up top, platelets and root ALT below.' Cut-offs: 1.3 = 'one-three, fibrosis-free'; 2.67 = 'refer'.

items.gloss_md: The standard liver panel: transaminases (ALT, AST) for hepatocellular injury, ALP and GGT for cholestasis, bilirubin for excretion, and albumin and INR (plus cholinesterase in Germany) for synthetic function.
items.body_md:
'Liver function tests' is a misnomer. Only bilirubin, albumin and INR (and cholinesterase) reflect function; the enzymes reflect injury.

- Hepatocellular pattern: ALT/AST predominantly raised (viral, toxic, ischaemic, autoimmune hepatitis, MASLD).
- Cholestatic pattern: ALP and GGT predominantly raised (PBC, PSC, obstruction, drugs, infiltration).
- Mixed: both. The R ratio quantifies the pattern.
- Synthetic failure (low albumin, high INR, low CHE, high bilirubin) signals advanced disease or acute liver failure. These parameters enter Child-Pugh and MELD.
- Normal enzymes do not exclude cirrhosis. Many patients with MASLD and even cirrhosis have normal ALT.

attrs.mnemonic: Two groups: 'injury' (ALT, AST = hepatocyte; ALP, GGT = bile duct) and 'function' (bilirubin, albumin, INR). Only the second group truly measures function.

items.gloss_md: The progressive, inflammatory form of MASLD: steatosis with lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning, with or without fibrosis. It replaces the term NASH.
items.body_md:
- Histological diagnosis: steatosis (≥5% of hepatocytes) + lobular inflammation + hepatocyte ballooning (often with Mallory–Denk bodies). It typically starts in zone 3, with perisinusoidal ('chicken-wire') fibrosis.
- Graded and staged with NAS (Kleiner/NASH CRN) or SAF/FLIP. Fibrosis staged F0–F4.
- Roughly a fifth to a third of people with MASLD have MASH. 'At-risk MASH' (NAS ≥4 and F≥2) is the target population of drug trials and can be estimated non-invasively (e.g. FAST score).
- Pathophysiology: 'multiple hits'. Insulin resistance, adipose-tissue lipolysis, de novo lipogenesis, lipotoxicity, ER and oxidative stress, gut microbiome and genetics lead to hepatocyte death, inflammation and stellate-cell activation.
- Regulatory endpoints: MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis, or fibrosis improvement by at least one stage without worsening of MASH.
- Drugs: resmetirom (approved 2024 US, 2025 EU, for F2–F3) and semaglutide (FDA 2025). Lifestyle remains the basis of treatment.

attrs.mnemonic: MASH = MASLD + 'H' for Hepatitis. Histology triad 'SIB': Steatosis, Inflammation (lobular), Ballooning.
attrs.anecdote: Jurgen Ludwig and colleagues at the Mayo Clinic coined 'nonalcoholic steatohepatitis' in 1980 for 20 patients whose biopsies looked like alcoholic hepatitis although they denied drinking.

items.gloss_md: Selection criteria for liver transplantation in HCC: a single tumour ≤5 cm or up to 3 tumours each ≤3 cm, without macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Within these limits, survival after transplantation is about 75% at 4–5 years with low recurrence.
items.body_md:
- Published by Vincenzo Mazzaferro et al. (NEJM 1996) from 48 patients in Milan: 4-year survival 75%, recurrence-free survival 83%.
- The worldwide standard for HCC transplant eligibility. In Eurotransplant/Germany, HCC within Milan (in cirrhosis) qualifies for MELD standard exception points.
- 'Downstaging': patients beyond Milan treated with TACE or ablation into Milan can be transplanted with comparable outcomes in many protocols.
- Criticised as too strict. Expanded criteria: UCSF, up-to-seven, AFP-based models (French AFP model, Metroticket 2.0).

attrs.mnemonic: '1 × 5 or 3 × 3': one up to 5 cm, or up to three up to 3 cm.
attrs.anecdote: Mazzaferro's 1996 NEJM paper was based on only 48 patients, yet it became one of the most influential selection rules in transplantation and has been used for listing decisions worldwide for decades.

items.gloss_md: Ultrasound-based method that measures liver stiffness (in kPa) from the speed of a mechanically induced shear wave. It is the most widely used non-invasive test for fibrosis and portal hypertension (device: FibroScan, Echosens).
items.body_md:
- Principle: a vibrator sends a low-frequency shear wave through the liver. Ultrasound tracks its speed, and speed is converted to Young's modulus (kPa). Normal is about 4–5 kPa. Range is 1.5–75 kPa.
- Quality: 10 valid measurements; IQR/median ≤30%. M probe standard, XL probe for obesity.
- MASLD (EASL 2021/2024): below 8 kPa rules out advanced fibrosis; 8–12 kPa grey zone; above 12 kPa advanced fibrosis likely (≥15 kPa suggests cirrhosis).
- Baveno VII: below 10 kPa rules out cACLD; above 15 highly suggestive; ≥25 kPa CSPH.
- Confounders that falsely raise stiffness: high ALT/acute hepatitis, congestion (heart failure), cholestasis, recent food intake (fast ≥2–3 h), alcohol use.
- Simultaneously measures CAP for steatosis. Combined scores: FAST (LSM + CAP + AST) for at-risk MASH, Agile 3+/4.
- Introduced commercially in the early 2000s.

attrs.mnemonic: Stiffer liver, faster wave: kPa thresholds in MASLD '8 and 12', in Baveno '10, 15, 25'.

items.gloss_md: Cirrhosis is 'compensated' until the first overt complication, and 'decompensated' once ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice appear. This transition sharply worsens prognosis.
items.body_md:
- Compensated: no ascites, no bleeding, no overt HE. Median survival over 12 years. Subdivided by presence of clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) and varices.
- Decompensated: median survival about 2 years. Ascites is the most common first decompensating event.
- D'Amico clinical stages: 1 = no varices, no ascites; 2 = varices; 3 = ascites ± varices; 4 = bleeding ± ascites. Later extensions add further decompensation stages.
- Baveno VII (2022) introduced 'recompensation': resolution of ascites, HE and bleeding off treatment after the cause has been removed (for example HCV cure or abstinence), with improved liver function.
- Prevention of decompensation in CSPH: non-selective beta-blockers, preferably carvedilol (PREDESCI trial).
- Acute decompensation can progress to ACLF.

attrs.mnemonic: Decompensation = 'A-B-E-J': Ascites, Bleeding (varices), Encephalopathy, Jaundice.

items.gloss_md: Cytosolic enzyme found predominantly in hepatocytes, whose serum level is the most liver-specific routine marker of hepatocellular injury.
items.body_md:
Catalyses the transfer of an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate (pyruvate + glutamate). Encoded by GPT (ALT1).

- Older name: SGPT (serum glutamate-pyruvate transaminase). In Germany it is still often called GPT.
- Half-life in serum is about 2 days, longer than AST.
- Upper limits of normal are lower than many labs use: the ACG suggests about 29–33 U/L for men and 19–25 U/L for women.
- Very high values (over 1000 U/L) suggest acute viral hepatitis, ischaemic hepatitis ('shock liver') or toxic injury (paracetamol). Moderate rises are typical of MASLD, chronic viral hepatitis and drugs.
- Used in FIB-4, APRI (via AST), the R ratio for DILI and Hy's law, and as an endpoint in clinical trials.

attrs.mnemonic: ALT = 'Liver' Transaminase: the L stands for Liver-specific. AST is in the heart and muscle too.

items.gloss_md: Yellow breakdown product of haem that the liver conjugates (UGT1A1) and excretes into bile. A raised serum level causes jaundice and reflects haemolysis, impaired conjugation or excretion, or cholestasis.
items.body_md:
- Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is albumin-bound and raised in haemolysis and in Gilbert syndrome (reduced UGT1A1 activity, about 5–10% of people, harmless).
- Conjugated (direct) bilirubin is raised in hepatocellular disease and cholestasis. It is water-soluble and appears in urine (dark urine).
- Normal total is below about 1.2 mg/dL (20 µmol/L). Conversion: 1 mg/dL = 17.1 µmol/L. Jaundice becomes visible at about 2.5–3 mg/dL.
- Prognostic in nearly all scores: Child-Pugh, MELD, Maddrey, Lille, ALBI, EAD criteria after transplantation, and the liver failure criterion in CLIF-C OF (≥12 mg/dL).

attrs.mnemonic: Indirect = Insoluble, Ill-attached to albumin (unconjugated). Direct = Dissolves in water (conjugated) and makes urine Dark.
attrs.anecdote: Gilbert syndrome was described by the French physician Augustin Gilbert in 1901. It is so common that mild jaundice after fasting or a cold is often the first time someone learns they have it.

items.gloss_md: Standardised prothrombin time ratio that reflects the hepatic synthesis of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. It is a key component of MELD and Child-Pugh.
items.body_md:
- INR = (patient PT / normal mean PT)^ISI. The ISI corrects for the thromboplastin reagent. It was designed for monitoring vitamin K antagonists, not for liver disease, so INR values from different labs vary in cirrhosis.
- Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), so INR rises within a day of acute liver failure. This makes it the key marker for defining ALF (INR ≥1.5 with encephalopathy).
- In cirrhosis, haemostasis is 'rebalanced' (pro- and anticoagulant factors both fall). A high INR does not predict procedural bleeding well, and routine correction with plasma before procedures is discouraged.
- Germany often reports the Quick value (%) alongside INR.

attrs.mnemonic: Factors II, VII, IX, X: '1972' (10, 9, 7, 2) — the vitamin K-dependent factors measured by the INR.

items.gloss_md: Transaminase found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and red cells (cytosolic and mitochondrial isoenzymes), so it is less liver-specific than ALT.
items.body_md:
- Older names: SGOT, and in Germany GOT.
- Half-life about 17 hours.
- Raised AST alone, without ALT, should prompt a look at muscle (CK), haemolysis or myocardial injury.
- The mitochondrial isoenzyme is released in alcohol-related injury. AST greater than ALT (De Ritis ratio over 1, often over 2) is typical of alcohol-associated liver disease and also of cirrhosis of any cause.
- Part of FIB-4, APRI, NAFLD fibrosis score and the AST/ALT ratio.

attrs.mnemonic: AST = 'All Sorts of Tissues' (liver, heart, muscle, red cells).

items.gloss_md: Perisinusoidal cell in the space of Disse that stores vitamin A when quiescent and, once activated, turns into a myofibroblast and is the main producer of scar tissue (extracellular matrix) in liver fibrosis.
items.body_md:
Quiescent stellate cells store retinyl esters in lipid droplets. Liver injury (from hepatocyte damage, Kupffer-cell signals, TGF-β, PDGF) activates them. They lose their vitamin A, express α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), proliferate, contract and secrete collagen I and III, and they produce TIMP-1, which blocks matrix breakdown.

- Activated HSCs are the central driver of fibrosis in all chronic liver diseases. Contraction of activated HSCs also adds to intrahepatic resistance in portal hypertension.
- When injury stops, they can revert or undergo apoptosis/senescence, which is why fibrosis can regress.
- Common single-cell markers: PDGFRB, DES, LRAT (quiescent), with ACTA2 and COL1A1 when activated.
- Antifibrotic drug development often targets HSC activation.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Stellate' = star: the star of fibrosis. Quiet star keeps vitamin A; activated star spits out collagen.
attrs.anecdote: They are also called Ito cells after Toshio Ito, who described fat-storing cells in the liver in the 1950s. Earlier, Karl Wilhelm von Kupffer had seen star-shaped cells in 1876 ('Sternzellen').

items.gloss_md: Removal of a small cylinder of liver tissue (percutaneously or transjugularly) for histology. It is the reference standard for grading and staging many liver diseases, including MASH in clinical trials, although non-invasive tests now replace it in most clinical decisions.
items.body_md:
- Routes: percutaneous (ultrasound-guided, 16–18 G needle); transjugular (for coagulopathy or ascites, can measure HVPG at the same time); surgical or laparoscopic.
- Adequacy: often at least 15–20 mm length and about 10–11 portal tracts.
- Limitations: sampling error (a biopsy is about 1/50,000 of the liver), inter-observer variability in reading, and complications (pain; bleeding in well under 1%; death very rare, about 1 in 10,000).
- Uses: unclear liver enzymes, autoimmune hepatitis (required for diagnosis), overlap syndromes, MASH staging (NAS, SAF, NASH CRN fibrosis), graft dysfunction after transplant (Banff rejection activity index), tumour diagnosis when imaging is atypical.
- Stains: H&E, Sirius red or trichrome (fibrosis), Perls (iron), rhodanine (copper), PAS-D (A1AT globules), CK7/CK19.
- Increasingly analysed by digital and AI pathology and spatial omics.

attrs.mnemonic: Biopsy = 'bios' (life) + 'opsis' (sight): a look at living tissue. But a liver biopsy sees only 1/50,000 of the organ — 'a keyhole view'.

items.gloss_md: The most abundant plasma protein, synthesised exclusively by hepatocytes. A low level is a marker of chronic liver dysfunction (and of malnutrition, inflammation and renal or intestinal loss).
items.body_md:
- Half-life about 3 weeks, so albumin reflects chronic rather than acute synthetic failure.
- Normal about 3.5–5 g/dL (35–50 g/L).
- Maintains oncotic pressure and binds bilirubin, drugs and hormones. Hypoalbuminaemia contributes to ascites and oedema.
- Part of Child-Pugh, ALBI, NAFLD fibrosis score, MELD 3.0 and the Lille model.
- Human albumin solution is used therapeutically in cirrhosis: after large-volume paracentesis, in SBP (prevents renal failure) and with terlipressin for HRS-AKI. Long-term albumin is debated (ANSWER trial favoured it, ATTIRE did not support targeting levels in hospital).

items.gloss_md: Enzyme from bile duct epithelium (and bone, placenta, intestine) whose serum rise is the main marker of cholestasis, for example in PBC, PSC or biliary obstruction.
items.body_md:
- Isoenzymes come from liver, bone, placenta and intestine. A raised ALP with raised GGT is hepatobiliary in origin. A raised ALP with normal GGT suggests bone (growth, Paget disease, metastases) or pregnancy.
- Cholestatic causes: PBC, PSC, obstruction (stones, PDAC of the pancreatic head, cholangiocarcinoma), infiltrative disease (metastases, granulomas, amyloid), drug-induced cholestasis, ductopenic rejection after liver transplant.
- In PBC, ALP (with bilirubin) defines treatment response to UDCA (for example the Paris II or POISE criteria, ALP below 1.67 × ULN).
- Unusually low ALP (with high bilirubin) is a clue to fulminant Wilson disease.

items.gloss_md: Membrane enzyme of biliary epithelium and hepatocytes. A raised serum level indicates cholestasis or enzyme induction (alcohol, drugs) and shows that a raised ALP comes from the liver.
items.body_md:
- Very sensitive but not specific: raised by alcohol, enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine), obesity/MASLD, cholestasis of any cause, and heart failure.
- Used to check the source of raised ALP: if ALP is high and GGT normal, think bone (or pregnancy/growth).
- GGT is used (with CDT, MCV and PEth) to monitor alcohol consumption, for example before and after liver transplantation for alcohol-associated liver disease.
- An independent predictor of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in population cohorts.

items.gloss_md: The main parenchymal cell of the liver (about 60–80% of liver cells and most of its mass) that carries out its metabolic, synthetic and detoxifying functions.
items.body_md:
Polarised epithelial cell with a basolateral (sinusoidal) side facing the space of Disse and an apical (canalicular) side forming bile canaliculi.

- Functions: synthesis of albumin and most clotting factors, glucose and lipid metabolism, urea cycle (ammonia detoxification), bile acid synthesis and secretion, bilirubin conjugation (UGT1A1), drug metabolism (CYP enzymes, e.g. CYP3A4).
- Injury releases ALT and AST into blood; loss of synthetic function shows as low albumin, prolonged INR and low cholinesterase.
- Lipid accumulation in hepatocytes is steatosis; swollen, rarefied hepatocytes ("ballooning") are a hallmark of steatohepatitis.
- Hepatocytes are normally quiescent but can proliferate rapidly after loss of liver mass (basis of resection and living-donor transplantation).

attrs.mnemonic: Hepato = liver, -cyte = cell: the hepatocyte is 'the' liver cell — when people say 'liver function', they mean hepatocyte function.
attrs.anecdote: The liver can regrow after two-thirds is removed, which is often linked to the Prometheus myth, in which an eagle ate the Titan's liver every day and it grew back each night.

items.gloss_md: Resident macrophage of the liver sinusoids, the largest tissue-macrophage population in the body, which clears gut-derived bacteria and endotoxin from portal blood.
items.body_md:
Kupffer cells sit inside the sinusoidal lumen, attached to the endothelium, mainly in periportal zones. They are self-renewing, embryonically derived tissue macrophages (marker examples: CD68, CLEC4F in mouse, VSIG4, MARCO). Recruited monocyte-derived macrophages are a different population.

- Function: phagocytosis of bacteria, LPS, old erythrocytes and debris; immune tolerance to gut antigens; iron recycling.
- In disease: they release TNF, IL-1β and ROS, which activate stellate cells. They drive ischaemia-reperfusion injury in transplantation and inflammation in alcohol-associated and metabolic liver disease.
- Single-cell studies of cirrhotic liver describe scar-associated macrophages (TREM2⁺ CD9⁺) that are distinct from Kupffer cells.

attrs.mnemonic: Kupffer catches bacteria like a 'cupper' (cup) in the sinusoid.
attrs.anecdote: Named after the German anatomist Karl Wilhelm von Kupffer, who in 1876 described them as 'Sternzellen' (star cells). Only in the late 1890s were they recognised as phagocytic macrophages rather than perisinusoidal 'star cells', a mix-up with what we now call stellate cells.

items.gloss_md: Ultrasound is the first-line tool for liver morphology, steatosis, ascites, Doppler flow and HCC surveillance. Multiphase contrast CT or MRI characterise focal lesions (LI-RADS) and stage tumours.
items.body_md:
- Ultrasound: steatosis (bright liver, reliable above about 20% fat), surface nodularity, splenomegaly, ascites, portal vein patency and flow direction (Doppler), bile duct dilatation. Cheap, no radiation, but operator-dependent and limited in obesity.
- Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) characterises lesions with microbubbles.
- Multiphase CT/MRI: arterial, portal venous and delayed phases. HCC can be diagnosed without biopsy by arterial hyperenhancement plus washout in high-risk patients.
- MRI with a hepatobiliary agent (gadoxetate, Primovist/Eovist) adds a hepatobiliary phase. MRCP shows bile ducts (PSC, strictures).
- MRI-PDFF quantifies liver fat. MR elastography measures stiffness and is often used as a trial endpoint.

items.gloss_md: Bundle at the corner of each liver lobule containing a branch of the portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery and a bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue (the portal tract).
items.body_md:
The portal tract also contains lymphatics and nerves, so 'portal triad' is a simplification.

- Blood from the portal vein (about 75% of inflow) and hepatic artery (about 25%) mixes in the sinusoids and flows towards the central vein. Bile flows the other way, towards the portal bile duct.
- Pathologists read many lesions relative to the portal tracts: portal and periportal fibrosis (early stages), interface hepatitis (inflammation crossing the limiting plate, typical of autoimmune hepatitis and chronic viral hepatitis), bile duct damage and loss (PBC, chronic rejection), and portal inflammation in T-cell mediated rejection of the liver.
- Biopsy adequacy is often stated as the number of portal tracts (for example 10 or more).
- In surgery, the hepatoduodenal ligament carries the 'big' triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, common bile duct). Clamping it is the Pringle manoeuvre.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) Glisson-Trias = 'V-A-D': Vena portae, Arteria hepatica, Ductus biliferus.

items.gloss_md: Division of the liver into eight functionally independent segments (I–VIII), each with its own portal pedicle and biliary drainage, separated by the hepatic veins. It is the basis of liver surgery and of describing lesion location on imaging.
items.body_md:
- The middle hepatic vein (Cantlie line, roughly gallbladder to IVC) divides the right lobe (V–VIII) from the left lobe (II–IV). The right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior (V, VIII) and posterior (VI, VII) sectors. The left hepatic vein and falciform ligament separate the left lateral (II, III) from the medial segment IV (IVa/IVb).
- Segment I (caudate lobe) drains directly into the IVC. It often hypertrophies in cirrhosis (Budd–Chiari too).
- Numbering runs clockwise from the caudate when viewed from the front: I, II, III, IV, then V, VI, VII, VIII.
- Relevance: anatomical resections (right hemihepatectomy = V–VIII), split liver (left lateral segment II+III for a child), living donation (right lobe V–VIII), LI-RADS and radiology reports ('lesion in segment VII').

attrs.mnemonic: Hold your hands in front of you as if holding the liver: numbers run clockwise from I (caudate), then II–III top-left, IV medial, V–VIII around the right lobe, with VIII ending up at the top right.
attrs.anecdote: Claude Couinaud, a French surgeon and anatomist, published the scheme in 1957 based on detailed studies of liver casts.

items.label_md: Dual blood supply of the liver
items.gloss_md: The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the portal vein (nutrient-rich, low-oxygen blood from gut and spleen) and about 25% from the hepatic artery (oxygen-rich), and drains through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.
items.body_md:
- Each source provides roughly half of the liver's oxygen.
- The bile ducts depend almost entirely on arterial supply. This is why hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplantation causes biliary necrosis and ischaemic-type strictures.
- HCC is fed mainly by the hepatic artery. This explains arterial-phase hyperenhancement with portal-venous washout on imaging and why TACE and SIRT work by arterial delivery.
- The hepatic arterial buffer response increases arterial flow when portal flow falls.
- The portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. This is relevant to PDAC resectability (portal/SMV involvement).

attrs.mnemonic: 'Three quarters portal, one quarter arterial — but the bile ducts only trust the artery.'

items.gloss_md: Epithelial cell lining the bile ducts that modifies bile (bicarbonate and water secretion) and is the target cell of cholangiopathies such as PBC and PSC and the cell of origin of cholangiocarcinoma.
items.body_md:
- Makes up only a few percent of liver cells but handles a large share of bile flow through secretin-stimulated bicarbonate secretion (CFTR, AE2). This forms the 'bicarbonate umbrella' that protects against toxic bile acids.
- Typical markers: KRT7, KRT19, SOX9, EPCAM.
- Damaged in primary biliary cholangitis (small ducts, autoimmune), primary sclerosing cholangitis (large and small ducts), ischaemic cholangiopathy after transplantation (DCD grafts), ductopenic chronic rejection and drug-induced cholestasis.
- 'Ductular reaction' (proliferating reactive ductules at the portal border) accompanies advanced fibrosis of many causes.

items.gloss_md: The ratio of AST to ALT. A ratio above 2 suggests alcohol-associated liver disease, and a ratio above 1 in chronic liver disease suggests advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
items.body_md:
- Normal and viral or metabolic hepatitis: usually below 1 (ALT predominant).
- Alcohol: often above 2. Mechanisms are mitochondrial AST release and pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) deficiency, which lowers ALT more than AST.
- Cirrhosis of any cause: AST tends to exceed ALT because AST clearance is reduced.
- Also elevated in Wilson disease presenting with acute liver failure.
- The ratio is a component of the NAFLD fibrosis score.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) 'De Ritis über 2 – Trinker im Spiel' (De Ritis above 2: alcohol is involved).
attrs.anecdote: Named after the Italian physician Fernando De Ritis, who described the ratio in 1957 in viral hepatitis.

items.label_md: Liver lobule, acinus and metabolic zonation
items.gloss_md: Microscopic organisation of the liver into hexagonal lobules around a central vein (or functional acini around portal tracts), with oxygen- and function-dependent zones 1 (periportal) to 3 (pericentral).
items.body_md:
- Zone 1 (periportal): highest oxygen, gluconeogenesis, β-oxidation, urea cycle. Iron in hereditary haemochromatosis is deposited here first.
- Zone 3 (pericentral or centrilobular): lowest oxygen, glutamine synthetase (marker GLUL), CYP2E1-rich. This zone is most sensitive to ischaemia and to paracetamol (NAPQI formation). Steatosis and ballooning in adult MASH start here, as does perisinusoidal ('chicken-wire') fibrosis.
- Zonation is maintained by Wnt/β-catenin signalling from central-vein endothelium. CTNNB1-mutated HCCs often express glutamine synthetase.
- Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell studies reconstruct zonation profiles in liver tissue.

attrs.mnemonic: Zone 3 is 'last in line' for oxygen, so it dies first in ischaemia and from paracetamol: 3 = Tod (death) zone.

items.gloss_md: German and Austrian way of reporting the prothrombin time as a percentage of normal activity (normal about 70–120%). A low Quick value means a prolonged prothrombin time, the opposite direction to the INR.
items.body_md:
- Quick % falls when INR rises. Roughly, Quick 50% corresponds to an INR of about 1.5, but the conversion depends on the reagent.
- Clinicians in German hospitals often say 'der Quick ist 40%' for impaired liver synthesis or anticoagulation with phenprocoumon (Marcumar).
- The MELD score requires the INR, not Quick, and the Child-Pugh score is defined on INR or PT seconds. German lab reports usually give both.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) 'Quick fällt, INR steigt': they move in opposite directions.
attrs.anecdote: Named after the American haematologist Armand J. Quick, who introduced the one-stage prothrombin time test in 1935.

items.gloss_md: Specialised endothelial cell lining the hepatic sinusoids, with open pores (fenestrae) and no basement membrane, so that plasma can reach hepatocytes directly.
items.body_md:
- Fenestrae of about 100–200 nm are grouped in sieve plates. Together with the missing basement membrane, they allow lipoproteins and plasma proteins to pass into the space of Disse.
- Scavenger function (clearance of macromolecules) and antigen presentation that tends to induce tolerance.
- Capillarisation (loss of fenestrae, formation of a basement membrane) is an early event in fibrosis. It impairs exchange and promotes portal hypertension.
- LSEC dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide raises intrahepatic vascular tone. LSECs are a primary target of ischaemia-reperfusion injury and of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (for example after oxaliplatin or HSCT conditioning).

items.gloss_md: R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN). It classifies liver injury as hepatocellular (R ≥5), cholestatic (R ≤2) or mixed (between 2 and 5), mainly in drug-induced liver injury.
items.body_md:
- Calculated from the first abnormal values. It guides the differential diagnosis and causality assessment (RUCAM uses different scales for hepatocellular and cholestatic/mixed injury).
- Hepatocellular DILI (for example isoniazid, many antiretrovirals) carries the Hy's law risk. Cholestatic DILI (for example amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids) resolves more slowly but is less often fatal.
- A 'new R' (nR) variant uses ALT or AST, whichever is higher.

attrs.mnemonic: R ≥5 = 'R'eally hepatocellular; R ≤2 = cholestatic; in between = mixed.

items.gloss_md: Butyrylcholinesterase made by the liver. In German clinical practice a low serum level is used as a sensitive marker of reduced hepatic synthetic function.
items.body_md:
- Also called pseudocholinesterase (gene BCHE). It is distinct from acetylcholinesterase at synapses.
- Short half-life (around 10 days), so it falls earlier than albumin when liver synthesis declines. It is also low in malnutrition and inflammation, and high in MASLD/obesity.
- Very commonly included in the German 'Leberwerte' panel ('Synthese: CHE, Albumin, Quick'). It is little used in the US.
- Genetic variants with low activity cause prolonged apnoea after succinylcholine.

items.gloss_md: The perisinusoidal space between the fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium and the hepatocytes, where plasma exchange takes place and hepatic stellate cells reside.
items.body_md:
- Contains hepatocyte microvilli, a sparse low-density matrix and stellate cells.
- In fibrosis, activated stellate cells deposit collagen here. Combined with loss of endothelial fenestrae (capillarisation), this blocks exchange between blood and hepatocytes and raises sinusoidal resistance.
- Lymph is formed from fluid in this space. Increased production in portal hypertension adds to ascites formation.

- Exchange of lipoproteins, albumin and drugs between blood and hepatocytes happens across this space, helped by hepatocyte microvilli.
- Loss of this exchange in cirrhosis contributes to impaired liver function beyond the loss of hepatocyte mass.

attrs.anecdote: Named after the German anatomist Joseph Disse (1852–1912).

items.gloss_md: Liver disease caused by chronic heavy alcohol intake, spanning steatosis, alcohol-associated hepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is the main cause of cirrhosis and of liver transplantation for cirrhosis in Germany.
items.body_md:
- Risk rises with dose and duration. Female sex, obesity/metabolic factors, PNPLA3 I148M, smoking and HBV/HCV increase the risk. Only a minority of heavy drinkers develop cirrhosis.
- Mechanisms: ethanol metabolism (ADH, CYP2E1) produces acetaldehyde and ROS, raises the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio and drives lipogenesis. Gut leakiness lets LPS reach Kupffer cells (TLR4), causing inflammation, neutrophil infiltration and fibrosis.
- Clues: AST/ALT >2, high GGT and MCV, CDT, PEth.
- Treatment: abstinence is by far the most important prognostic factor, even in cirrhosis. Addiction treatment (e.g. acamprosate, baclofen in cirrhosis), nutrition, and corticosteroids for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis.
- Liver transplantation: excellent results. Traditional requirement of 6 months' abstinence; selected early transplantation for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis in some centres. Relapse monitoring after transplant.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) In German reports you will read 'C2-toxisch' or 'äthyltoxisch' for alcohol-related (C2 = ethanol, two carbons).

items.label_md: Lifestyle intervention and weight loss in MASLD
items.gloss_md: The foundation of MASLD/MASH treatment: weight loss through diet and physical activity. About 7–10% body-weight loss improves steatohepatitis, and 10% or more can make fibrosis regress.
items.body_md:
- Dose-response (Vilar-Gomez et al., Gastroenterology 2015): weight loss ≥5% reduces steatosis; ≥7% resolves NASH in many; ≥10% leads to NASH resolution in about 90% and fibrosis regression in about 45%.
- Diet: hypocaloric, Mediterranean style; avoid fructose-sweetened drinks and ultra-processed food; reduce alcohol (best none in advanced fibrosis). Coffee consumption is associated with lower fibrosis.
- Exercise: 150–300 min/week of moderate aerobic activity or resistance training; improves steatosis even without weight loss.
- Bariatric/metabolic surgery leads to MASH resolution in most patients and is considered in obesity with MASH (not in decompensated cirrhosis).
- Treat comorbidities: diabetes (GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors), statins for cardiovascular risk (safe in compensated cirrhosis).
- Sustained adherence is the main problem: fewer than 10% of patients achieve and keep ≥10% weight loss.

attrs.mnemonic: '5 – 7 – 10': 5% loses fat, 7% calms the inflammation, 10% reverses scars.

items.gloss_md: The 2023 multisociety (AASLD, EASL, ALEH) nomenclature that uses 'steatotic liver disease' as the umbrella term and subdivides it into MASLD, MetALD, alcohol-associated liver disease, specific aetiologies and cryptogenic SLD.
items.body_md:
Published in June 2023 (Rinella et al., simultaneously in J Hepatol, Hepatology and Ann Hepatol) after a Delphi process.

- SLD (any steatosis) is divided into:
  - MASLD: ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor, alcohol below 140 g/week (women) or 210 g/week (men).
  - MetALD: MASLD criteria plus 140–350 g/week (women) or 210–420 g/week (men).
  - ALD (alcohol-associated/related liver disease): above these amounts.
  - Specific aetiology: drug-induced, monogenic (e.g. lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, Wilson disease), HCV genotype 3, malnutrition and others.
  - Cryptogenic SLD: no risk factor and no cause.
- NASH becomes MASH. 'Non-alcoholic' and 'fatty' were dropped as stigmatising.
- Over 95% of people with NAFLD meet MASLD criteria, so earlier NAFLD trial and cohort data remain valid.

attrs.mnemonic: Alcohol borders in grams per week: '140/210 – 350/420'. Women/men: below 140/210 = MASLD, up to 350/420 = MetALD, above = ALD.

items.label_md: GLP-1 receptor agonists in MASH (semaglutide, tirzepatide)
items.gloss_md: Incretin-based drugs for diabetes and obesity that reduce weight, liver fat and steatohepatitis. Semaglutide 2.4 mg/week received FDA accelerated approval for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis in 2025.
items.body_md:
- Semaglutide (Wegovy/Ozempic): ESSENCE phase 3 (Sanyal et al., NEJM 2025) at 72 weeks: MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening about 63% vs 34% (placebo); fibrosis improvement about 37% vs 22%.
- Mechanism: mostly indirect, through weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity. Hepatocytes express little GLP-1R.
- Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist; SYNERGY-NASH phase 2) and survodutide (glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist) also showed strong histological effects. Retatrutide (triple agonist) is in development.
- Also reduce cardiovascular events, the main cause of death in MASLD.
- Side effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, gallstones, loss of muscle mass.
- Recommended by EASL-EASD-EASO 2024 for MASLD patients with type 2 diabetes or obesity.

attrs.anecdote: GLP-1 drugs trace back to exendin-4, a peptide found in the venom of the Gila monster lizard by John Eng in the early 1990s. It became exenatide, the first GLP-1 receptor agonist (2005).

items.gloss_md: Oral liver-directed thyroid hormone receptor-β (THR-β) agonist. It was the first drug approved for MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis (F2–F3): FDA accelerated approval in March 2024, EU approval in 2025.
items.body_md:
- Trade name Rezdiffra (Madrigal). Dose 80 or 100 mg/day by body weight.
- Mechanism: THR-β is the main thyroid hormone receptor isoform in hepatocytes. Activation increases fatty-acid β-oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis and LDL clearance and reduces liver fat. It is selective to avoid THR-α effects (heart, bone).
- MAESTRO-NASH phase 3 (Harrison et al., NEJM 2024): at 52 weeks, NASH resolution about 26–30% vs 10% (placebo); fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage about 24–26% vs 14%. Also lowers LDL cholesterol.
- Side effects: diarrhoea, nausea. Interactions with CYP2C8 inhibitors and statin dose adjustment.
- Not approved in decompensated cirrhosis. Outcome trials (including compensated MASH cirrhosis, MAESTRO-NASH OUTCOMES) are ongoing.

attrs.mnemonic: Res-ME-TI-rom: it gives the liver its own 'metabolism boost' via the thyroid receptor beta — 'beta for the belly (liver), alpha for the heart'.

items.gloss_md: Acute-on-chronic inflammatory syndrome in heavy drinkers with recent onset of jaundice. Severe forms have a 90-day mortality of about 20–30% or more.
items.body_md:
- NIAAA clinical criteria: onset of jaundice within 8 weeks; ongoing heavy alcohol intake (over 40 g/day for women, over 60 g/day for men) for at least 6 months, with fewer than 60 days of abstinence before jaundice; bilirubin above 3 mg/dL; AST above 50 U/L, AST/ALT over 1.5, both below 400 U/L.
- Clinical features: fever, tender hepatomegaly and leukocytosis, so infection must be excluded.
- Histology: steatosis, ballooning, Mallory–Denk bodies, neutrophil infiltration, pericellular fibrosis.
- Severity: Maddrey DF ≥32 or MELD >20 = severe. Prednisolone 40 mg/day for 28 days is considered. Response is assessed at day 7 by the Lille model (≥0.45 = non-response, stop steroids). The STOPAH trial (2015) showed only a short-term (28-day) mortality trend, no long-term benefit.
- Mainstays: abstinence, nutrition, infection control.
- Early liver transplantation for selected non-responders (Mathurin et al., NEJM 2011) is now practised in some centres.

attrs.mnemonic: Steroid decision in two steps: 'Maddrey decides who starts (≥32), Lille decides who stops (≥0.45 on day 7)'.

items.gloss_md: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis: the pre-2023 names for MASLD and MASH. They were defined by exclusion of significant alcohol use and other causes rather than by metabolic risk factors.
items.body_md:
- NAFLD: steatosis in ≥5% of hepatocytes without significant alcohol use (traditionally below 20 g/day for women, 30 g/day for men) and without secondary causes.
- NASH: NAFLD with steatohepatitis. Term coined by Ludwig et al. (Mayo Clinic) in 1980.
- MAFLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease, Eslam et al. 2020) was an earlier alternative proposal with positive criteria. It allowed coexisting causes but was not adopted by the multisociety consensus.
- Most literature, drug trials (until about 2023), biobank phenotypes and ICD-10 codes (K75.8, K76.0) still use NAFLD/NASH. MASLD and NAFLD populations overlap by over 95%, so findings transfer.
- Expect both sets of terms in data sets, papers and clinician conversations.

attrs.mnemonic: N-words are out: NAFLD becomes MASLD and NASH becomes MASH — swap 'Non-alcoholic' for 'Metabolic'.

items.gloss_md: Prognostic score for alcohol-associated hepatitis: 4.6 × (patient's prothrombin time − control PT, in seconds) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). A value of 32 or more indicates severe disease, where corticosteroids are considered.
items.body_md:
- DF ≥32 corresponds to a high short-term mortality without treatment (historically about 30–50% at one month).
- Uses PT in seconds, not INR, so it varies with the lab reagent. MELD above 20 is used as an alternative criterion for severe AH.
- Developed by Maddrey et al. (1978); modified in 1989 (factor 4.6) for the steroid trial.
- Response to steroids is checked after 7 days by the Lille model.

attrs.mnemonic: '4.6 times the PT delay plus bilirubin; 32 or more — think steroids.'

items.gloss_md: Steatotic liver disease category for people who meet MASLD criteria and also drink moderately to heavily: 140–350 g/week (women) or 210–420 g/week (men).
items.body_md:
- Introduced by the 2023 SLD nomenclature to recognise the continuum between metabolic and alcohol-related disease.
- Within MetALD, the contribution can lean towards MASLD or towards ALD.
- Alcohol intake should be measured objectively if possible (AUDIT-C questionnaire, PEth, ethyl glucuronide), because self-report underestimates it.
- MetALD has a higher risk of fibrosis progression and mortality than MASLD alone. Alcohol and metabolic factors act synergistically, especially with PNPLA3 risk alleles.

items.gloss_md: Score calculated after 7 days of corticosteroids in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, from age, albumin, creatinine, prothrombin time, baseline bilirubin and the change in bilirubin. A score of 0.45 or more means non-response, and steroids should be stopped.
items.body_md:
- Range 0–1. A score ≥0.45 predicts 6-month survival of about 25%, versus about 85% in responders (Louvet et al., 2007).
- Responses can be refined by Lille thresholds (≤0.16 complete, 0.16–0.56 partial, ≥0.56 null).
- Non-responders: stop steroids (infection risk). Selected patients are considered for early liver transplantation.
- Named after the French city (Université de Lille), where it was developed.

attrs.mnemonic: Lille on day 7: 'bilirubin should fall in a week — if Lille is 0.45 or more, steroids go.'

items.gloss_md: Accumulation of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. In about 80% of cases it is due to cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and in cirrhosis it is the most common decompensating event.
items.body_md:
- Pathophysiology: portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation reduce effective arterial blood volume. RAAS, sympathetic and ADH activation then cause sodium and water retention. Hypoalbuminaemia contributes.
- Grades (International Ascites Club): 1 = detectable only on ultrasound; 2 = moderate, symmetrical abdominal distension; 3 = large/tense.
- Diagnostic paracentesis for every new ascites and every hospital admission: cell count (SBP: neutrophils ≥250/µL), albumin for SAAG, total protein, culture in blood-culture bottles, cytology if indicated.
- Treatment: moderate salt restriction (about 5 g salt/day), spironolactone ± furosemide, large-volume paracentesis with albumin, TIPS for refractory or recurrent ascites, liver transplantation.
- Refractory ascites (non-responsive to or intolerant of diuretics) indicates poor prognosis.

attrs.mnemonic: SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension ('high gradient, high pressure'). Low SAAG means peritoneal disease (cancer, TB, pancreatitis).

items.gloss_md: Reversible brain dysfunction caused by liver insufficiency and/or portosystemic shunting, ranging from minimal cognitive deficits to coma, with ammonia playing a central role.
items.body_md:
- Pathophysiology: gut-derived ammonia (and other toxins) bypasses the liver. Astrocytes detoxify it into glutamine, which causes osmotic swelling. Systemic inflammation, benzodiazepine-like substances and altered neurotransmission add to the effect.
- Grades: West Haven 0–4. Covert HE = minimal HE + grade 1; overt HE = grade ≥2. Asterixis ('flapping tremor') appears in grade 2.
- Precipitants (found in most episodes): infection (including SBP), GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration/diuretics, hypokalaemia/hyponatraemia, sedatives, TIPS.
- Diagnosis is clinical, excluding other causes. Venous ammonia helps mainly by its negative predictive value. Minimal HE is detected with psychometric tests (PHES, Stroop app, CFF).
- Treatment: correct the precipitant; lactulose (titrated to 2–3 soft stools per day); rifaximin added for prevention of recurrence; LOLA or PEG as alternatives. Avoid protein restriction. Recurrent HE is an indication to evaluate for liver transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: HE precipitants 'BICEPS': Bleeding, Infection, Constipation, Electrolytes/dehydration, Psychoactive drugs (sedatives), Shunt (TIPS).

items.gloss_md: Interventional radiology procedure that places a covered stent through the liver between a hepatic vein and a portal vein branch, via the jugular vein, to decompress portal hypertension.
items.body_md:
- Indications: refractory or recurrent ascites; acute variceal bleeding (pre-emptive within 72 h in high-risk patients, or as rescue); secondary prophylaxis of bleeding; hepatic hydrothorax; Budd–Chiari; selected portal vein thrombosis.
- Today PTFE-covered stents are used (better patency). Controlled-expansion stents allow smaller diameters (8 mm).
- Target portosystemic gradient below 12 mmHg.
- Complications: hepatic encephalopathy (the most important, in a substantial share of patients), heart failure (increased preload), liver failure, shunt dysfunction.
- Contraindications: severe heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, recurrent overt HE, high bilirubin/MELD (often MELD >18–20 relative), uncontrolled infection.
- Pre-emptive TIPS improved survival after variceal bleeding in Child C 10–13 / B with active bleeding (García-Pagán et al., NEJM 2010).

attrs.mnemonic: TIPS = a 'Tunnel In the Parenchyma' that lets portal blood Skip the liver: good for pressure (ascites, bleeding), bad for the brain (HE, the ammonia skips the liver too).
attrs.anecdote: TIPS was first proposed by Josef Rösch in the late 1960s after he accidentally punctured the portal vein during a transjugular cholangiogram. The first clinical stent-based TIPS was performed in Freiburg, Germany, in 1988 (Richter, Palmaz and colleagues).

items.gloss_md: Drugs that lower portal pressure by reducing cardiac output (β1) and splanchnic inflow (β2 blockade leaving α-vasoconstriction unopposed). They are used to prevent variceal bleeding and, per Baveno VII, decompensation in clinically significant portal hypertension. Carvedilol is preferred.
items.body_md:
- Carvedilol (6.25–12.5 mg/day) also blocks α1 receptors, which reduces intrahepatic resistance. It lowers HVPG more than propranolol.
- PREDESCI trial (Villanueva et al., Lancet 2019): NSBB reduced decompensation (mainly ascites) in compensated cirrhosis with CSPH.
- Uses: primary prophylaxis (alternative: band ligation), secondary prophylaxis combined with band ligation, prevention of decompensation in CSPH.
- 'Window hypothesis': in refractory ascites, hypotension (systolic BP below 90 mmHg), hyponatraemia or AKI, reduce the dose or stop the drug.
- Propranolol is titrated to resting heart rate 55–60/min. Avoid in asthma.

attrs.mnemonic: Carvedilol = 'Car' with two brakes: β-blockade lowers inflow and α1-blockade relaxes the liver, so it lowers portal pressure more than propranolol.

items.gloss_md: Dilated portosystemic collateral veins in the distal oesophagus or stomach that develop with portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg) and can rupture and bleed.
items.body_md:
- Found in about half of patients with cirrhosis. They form at an HVPG of 10 mmHg or more and can bleed from 12 mmHg.
- Screening by upper GI endoscopy (EGD). It can be skipped under the Baveno VI criteria (LSM below 20 kPa and platelets above 150 × 10⁹/L). Under Baveno VII, patients with CSPH should simply receive carvedilol.
- Grading: small vs large (over 5 mm). Red wale marks and Child-Pugh C increase bleeding risk.
- Gastric varices are classified by Sarin (GOV1/2, IGV1/2) and treated with cyanoacrylate injection or TIPS/BRTO.
- Primary prophylaxis: non-selective beta-blocker (carvedilol, propranolol) or endoscopic band ligation. Secondary prophylaxis after bleeding: both combined.

attrs.mnemonic: Varices form at an HVPG of 10 and bleed from 12: '10 to form, 12 to bleed'.

items.gloss_md: Haemorrhage from ruptured oesophageal or gastric varices. It is a medical emergency with a 6-week mortality of about 15–20%, managed with vasoactive drugs, antibiotics, endoscopic band ligation and, in high-risk patients, pre-emptive TIPS.
items.body_md:
Management bundle (Baveno VII):

- Restrictive transfusion: target haemoglobin about 7–8 g/dL, since over-transfusion raises portal pressure.
- Vasoactive drugs as soon as bleeding is suspected (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide) for 2–5 days.
- Antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. ceftriaxone 1 g/day, up to 7 days) reduces infection, rebleeding and death.
- Endoscopy within 12 hours, with band ligation (oesophageal) or cyanoacrylate (gastric). Erythromycin before endoscopy improves the view.
- Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h (ideally 24 h) in high-risk patients: Child-Pugh C 10–13, or Child-Pugh B >7 with active bleeding at endoscopy.
- Rescue: balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore, Linton–Nachlas) or a self-expanding oesophageal stent (Danis) as a bridge to rescue TIPS.
- Lactulose to prevent HE. Afterwards, secondary prophylaxis with NSBB plus band ligation.

attrs.mnemonic: Bleeding bundle 'VAEB': Vasoactive drug, Antibiotics, Endoscopy within 12 h, Bands, then pre-emptive TIPS if high-risk.

items.gloss_md: Syndrome of acute decompensation of chronic liver disease (usually cirrhosis) with organ failure(s) and high short-term mortality. In Europe it is defined by EASL-CLIF using the CLIF-C organ failure score.
items.body_md:
EASL-CLIF definition (CANONIC study, Moreau et al. 2013). Organ failures are assessed in 6 systems: liver (bilirubin ≥12 mg/dL), kidney (creatinine ≥2 mg/dL or renal replacement), brain (HE grade 3–4), coagulation (INR ≥2.5), circulation (vasopressors), respiration (PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤200 or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤214).

- Grade 1: single kidney failure; or single other organ failure with creatinine 1.5–1.9 mg/dL and/or HE grade 1–2.
- Grade 2: two organ failures.
- Grade 3: three or more organ failures.
- 28-day mortality in CANONIC: about 22% (grade 1), 32% (grade 2) and 77% (grade 3), versus about 5% without ACLF.

Triggers: bacterial infection, alcohol-associated hepatitis, GI bleeding, HBV flare; often no trigger is found. Pathophysiology: systemic inflammation. The CLIF-C ACLF score (organ failure score plus age plus white cell count) refines prognosis. Other definitions exist (APASL in Asia-Pacific, NACSELD in North America). Urgent liver transplantation can rescue selected grade 3 patients.

attrs.mnemonic: Six organs of CLIF-C OF = 'LKBCCR': Liver, Kidney, Brain, Coagulation, Circulation, Respiration. Grade = number of organ failures (with the kidney special rule for grade 1).

items.gloss_md: Functional acute kidney injury in advanced cirrhosis with ascites, caused by intense renal vasoconstriction in response to splanchnic vasodilation. It is diagnosed when AKI does not respond to volume expansion and has no structural kidney cause.
items.body_md:
ICA criteria (2015) for HRS-AKI:

- Cirrhosis with ascites.
- AKI by ICA criteria: serum creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥50% within 7 days.
- No response after 2 consecutive days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin (1 g/kg/day).
- No shock and no current or recent nephrotoxic drugs.
- No signs of structural kidney injury: proteinuria ≤500 mg/day, ≤50 red cells per high-power field, normal kidney ultrasound.

The former 'type 1 HRS' is now HRS-AKI. The former 'type 2' is HRS-NAKI (HRS-AKD/CKD). The 2024 ADQI/ICA update adds urine output criteria.

Treatment: terlipressin plus albumin (norepinephrine in the ICU as an alternative). Response is about 40–50%. Definitive therapy is liver transplantation, with combined liver-kidney transplantation if renal recovery is unlikely. Untreated prognosis is weeks.

attrs.anecdote: Kidneys of patients who died with hepatorenal syndrome were successfully transplanted into other recipients and worked normally (Koppel et al., NEJM 1969). Likewise, kidney function usually recovers after liver transplantation. This proved that HRS is functional and the kidney itself is intact.

items.gloss_md: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source, diagnosed by an ascitic neutrophil count of 250/µL or more. It is a frequent, life-threatening complication of cirrhotic ascites.
items.body_md:
- Pathogenesis: bacterial translocation from the gut (mostly Gram-negative Enterobacterales, increasingly Gram-positive and multidrug-resistant organisms in hospital), with low ascitic opsonic activity.
- Often oligosymptomatic. Can present as worsening HE, AKI or fever only, hence diagnostic paracentesis at every admission.
- Treatment: empirical third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) in community-acquired cases, broader cover (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem) in nosocomial cases. Plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3, which reduces HRS and mortality (Sort et al., NEJM 1999).
- Secondary prophylaxis after an episode: norfloxacin (or ciprofloxacin, or cotrimoxazole). One-year recurrence without prophylaxis is about 70%.
- Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforation) has very high neutrophil counts and polymicrobial culture.

attrs.mnemonic: SBP threshold 250 = 'two-fifty means the belly is infected'. Treatment: 'Cef + Alb 1.5 then 1': a cephalosporin plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3.

items.gloss_md: Needle drainage of ascitic fluid, either diagnostic (cell count, culture, albumin, protein) or therapeutic (large-volume paracentesis, LVP, often more than 5 L), followed by albumin infusion.
items.body_md:
- Diagnostic paracentesis for every new ascites and every hospital admission of a patient with ascites (to exclude SBP). Coagulopathy is not a contraindication.
- Large-volume paracentesis: treatment of tense or refractory ascites. With more than 5 L removed, give albumin 6–8 g per litre removed (e.g. 20% albumin) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (PPCD), which causes hyponatraemia, renal impairment and higher mortality.
- Long-term alternatives: TIPS, the alfapump (automated pump to the bladder), liver transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: '8 grams per litre after 5 litres': albumin rule after large-volume paracentesis.

items.gloss_md: Non-absorbable synthetic disaccharide (galactose-fructose) that is first-line treatment and secondary prophylaxis of hepatic encephalopathy. It acidifies the colon, traps ammonia as ammonium and acts as a laxative.
items.body_md:
- Colonic bacteria ferment lactulose to short-chain acids. The lower pH converts NH₃ to NH₄⁺, which is not absorbed, and shifts flora away from urease producers. The osmotic laxative effect clears the gut.
- Dose: titrate to 2–3 soft bowel movements per day (orally or as an enema in coma).
- Secondary prophylaxis after the first episode of overt HE. Also given after variceal bleeding.
- Overdosing causes dehydration and hypernatraemia, which can worsen HE.
- Lactitol is an alternative. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) was faster than lactulose for acute HE in one trial.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Two to three soft stools a day keep the ammonia away.'

items.gloss_md: Vasopressin analogue (prodrug of lysine vasopressin) that constricts splanchnic vessels. It is used for acute variceal bleeding and, together with albumin, for hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI).
items.body_md:
- V1 receptor agonist: splanchnic vasoconstriction lowers portal inflow and pressure and raises effective arterial volume, which improves renal perfusion.
- Variceal bleeding: 2 mg every 4 h IV initially, then titrated, for 2–5 days.
- HRS-AKI: bolus or continuous infusion (continuous infusion has fewer side effects) + albumin 20–40 g/day. Response is a creatinine fall to below 1.5 mg/dL. CONFIRM trial led to US approval (Terlivaz, 2022). Long used in Europe (Glycylpressin, Haemopressin).
- Side effects: ischaemia (cardiac, mesenteric, digital, skin), hyponatraemia, respiratory failure/fluid overload (especially with ACLF grade 3 or high creatinine).
- Alternatives: norepinephrine (HRS in ICU); somatostatin/octreotide (bleeding).

attrs.mnemonic: Terlipressin 'presses' the splanchnic vessels: less portal inflow (bleeding stops) and more blood for the kidneys (HRS).

items.gloss_md: Clinical grading of overt hepatic encephalopathy from grade 0 to 4, based on mental state, behaviour and consciousness.
items.body_md:
- Grade 0: no clinical signs (minimal HE detectable only by psychometric tests).
- Grade 1: trivial lack of awareness, euphoria or anxiety, shortened attention span, impaired addition/subtraction, altered sleep rhythm.
- Grade 2: lethargy or apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis.
- Grade 3: somnolence to semi-stupor, responsive to stimuli, confusion, gross disorientation, bizarre behaviour.
- Grade 4: coma.

ISHEN groups minimal HE and grade 1 as 'covert HE' and grades 2–4 as 'overt HE'. HE grades enter Child-Pugh (1–2 vs 3–4) and CLIF-C OF (brain failure = grade 3–4).

attrs.mnemonic: 1 = 'odd' (sleep, attention), 2 = 'disoriented + flapping' (asterixis), 3 = 'drowsy', 4 = 'coma'. Covert up to 1, overt from 2.
attrs.anecdote: Named after West Haven, Connecticut, where Harold Conn and colleagues at the Yale-affiliated VA hospital developed the grading in the 1970s for a lactulose trial.

items.gloss_md: Poorly absorbed oral rifamycin antibiotic. Added to lactulose, it prevents recurrence of overt hepatic encephalopathy.
items.body_md:
- 550 mg twice daily. Bass et al. (NEJM 2010): reduced HE recurrence and HE-related hospitalisations over 6 months (most patients also on lactulose).
- Acts in the gut lumen (less than 0.4% absorbed), modulating the microbiome and reducing ammonia-producing bacteria and endotoxin.
- Trade names Xifaxan, Xifaxan 550. Also used for travellers' diarrhoea and IBS with diarrhoea.
