- Being studied for prevention of other complications (SBP, infections) with mixed results.

items.gloss_md: Baveno term for the spectrum of advanced fibrosis and compensated cirrhosis in asymptomatic patients, defined non-invasively mainly by liver stiffness on transient elastography.
items.body_md:
- Introduced by Baveno VI (2015) and refined in Baveno VII (2022). The term acknowledges that F3 and F4 cannot be distinguished reliably without biopsy.
- Liver stiffness (LSM by transient elastography): below 10 kPa (without other signs) rules out cACLD; 10–15 kPa is suggestive; above 15 kPa is highly suggestive.
- Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH): LSM ≥25 kPa rules it in. LSM ≤15 kPa with platelets ≥150 × 10⁹/L rules it out.
- 'Baveno VI criteria': LSM below 20 kPa and platelets above 150 × 10⁹/L mean a low probability of high-risk varices, so screening endoscopy can be avoided.
- Specific rules apply to obesity-related MASLD (the ANTICIPATE models).

attrs.mnemonic: Baveno 'rule of five' for kPa: 10 – 15 – 20 – 25. Below 10 no cACLD, above 15 cACLD likely, below 20 (with platelets above 150) skip endoscopy, from 25 CSPH.
attrs.anecdote: The Baveno consensus workshops on portal hypertension are named after the small town of Baveno on Lake Maggiore in Italy, where the first meeting was held in 1990.

items.gloss_md: Endoscopic placement of rubber bands around oesophageal varices to strangulate and obliterate them. It is the endoscopic treatment of choice for acute oesophageal variceal bleeding and for prophylaxis.
items.body_md:
- Repeated every 2–4 weeks until varices are eradicated, then surveillance.
- Superior to sclerotherapy (fewer complications). Post-banding ulcer bleeding is the main complication (PPI helps).
- Primary prophylaxis: alternative to NSBB in large varices. Secondary prophylaxis: combined with NSBB.
- Gastric (fundal) varices: cyanoacrylate glue injection instead.

- In acute bleeding, EBL is performed during the emergency endoscopy (within 12 h) together with vasoactive drugs and antibiotics. If bleeding cannot be controlled, a balloon tamponade or oesophageal stent bridges to rescue TIPS.
- Band ligation lowers bleeding risk locally but does not lower portal pressure, so it does not prevent ascites or other decompensation. This is one reason Baveno VII prefers carvedilol when CSPH is present.

items.gloss_md: Invasive reference measurement of portal pressure: wedged hepatic venous pressure minus free hepatic venous pressure, measured with a balloon catheter via the jugular vein.
items.body_md:
- Normal 1–5 mmHg; CSPH ≥10 mmHg; variceal bleeding risk ≥12 mmHg.
- Reflects sinusoidal pressure, so it underestimates presinusoidal hypertension (e.g. portal vein thrombosis, schistosomiasis).
- Haemodynamic response to beta-blockers (a fall of ≥10–20% or to below 12 mmHg) predicts lower bleeding and decompensation risk.
- Used as an endpoint in trials and in specialised centres. Often combined with transjugular liver biopsy.
- Non-invasive surrogates: liver and spleen stiffness, platelet count.

items.gloss_md: Thrombosis of the portal vein, either bland (common in cirrhosis because of slow flow) or tumour thrombus (macrovascular invasion of HCC, BCLC C).
items.body_md:
- In cirrhosis, prevalence increases with severity. It can worsen portal hypertension and complicate liver transplantation (the extent is graded by Yerdel).
- Non-cirrhotic PVT: look for myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2 V617F), thrombophilia, abdominal inflammation (pancreatitis) or malignancy (PDAC).
- Bland vs tumour thrombus: tumour thrombus enhances in the arterial phase and expands the vein.
- Treatment: anticoagulation (LMWH, VKA or DOACs in Child A/B) in recent PVT and LT candidates. TIPS for selected cases.
- Chronic PVT leads to 'cavernous transformation' (portal cavernoma).

items.label_md: CLIF-C organ failure and ACLF scores
items.gloss_md: Scores from the EASL-CLIF Consortium: CLIF-C OF grades failure of six organ systems (liver, kidney, brain, coagulation, circulation, lungs) and defines ACLF. CLIF-C ACLF adds age and white cell count for prognosis.
items.body_md:
- CLIF-C OF assigns 1–3 points per organ (total 6–18) based on bilirubin, creatinine/RRT, HE grade, INR, mean arterial pressure/vasopressors, PaO₂/FiO₂ or SpO₂/FiO₂.
- CLIF-C ACLF = 10 × [0.33 × CLIF-C OFs + 0.04 × age + 0.63 × ln(WBC) − 2]. A score above 70 after 3–7 days of ICU care in ACLF-3 is often cited as indicating futility of further intensive care.
- CLIF-C AD score: for acute decompensation without ACLF.
- CLIF stands for Chronic Liver Failure.

items.gloss_md: Two pulmonary vascular complications of portal hypertension: hepatopulmonary syndrome (intrapulmonary vasodilation causing hypoxaemia) and portopulmonary hypertension (pulmonary arterial hypertension).
items.body_md:
- Hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS): liver disease/portal hypertension + intrapulmonary vascular dilations (shown by contrast/bubble echocardiography with late left-sided bubbles) + impaired oxygenation (A–a gradient ≥15 mmHg). Platypnoea-orthodeoxia is typical. Severe HPS is an indication for liver transplantation (MELD standard exception), after which it usually resolves.
- Portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH): precapillary pulmonary hypertension in portal hypertension. Screened by echocardiography and confirmed by right heart catheter. Severe PoPH (high mPAP/PVR not responding to therapy) is a contraindication to liver transplantation because of perioperative mortality.

attrs.mnemonic: HPS = too wide vessels (low oxygen, LT cures it). PoPH = too narrow vessels (high pressure, LT may kill). Opposite problems, opposite meaning for transplantation.

items.gloss_md: Serum albumin minus ascitic albumin. A value of 1.1 g/dL or more indicates portal-hypertensive ascites with about 97% accuracy.
items.body_md:
- SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL (11 g/L): cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd–Chiari, massive liver metastases.
- SAAG below 1.1 g/dL: peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome.
- Ascitic total protein helps further: high protein (≥2.5 g/dL) with high SAAG suggests cardiac ascites or Budd–Chiari. Low protein (below 1.5 g/dL) in cirrhosis increases SBP risk (an indication for primary prophylaxis in some guidelines).
- SAAG replaced the older exudate/transudate classification.

items.label_md: NAFLD activity score (NAS) and NASH CRN fibrosis staging
items.gloss_md: Histological scoring system of the NASH Clinical Research Network (Kleiner et al., 2005): NAS = steatosis (0–3) + lobular inflammation (0–3) + ballooning (0–2), total 0–8, with a separate fibrosis stage 0–4.
items.body_md:
- Steatosis: 0 (<5%), 1 (5–33%), 2 (34–66%), 3 (>66%).
- Lobular inflammation (foci per 200× field): 0 none, 1 (<2), 2 (2–4), 3 (>4).
- Ballooning: 0 none, 1 few, 2 many.
- Fibrosis: 0 none; 1a mild zone 3 perisinusoidal; 1b moderate zone 3 perisinusoidal; 1c portal/periportal only; 2 zone 3 perisinusoidal + portal/periportal; 3 bridging; 4 cirrhosis.

NAS ≥5 correlated with a diagnosis of steatohepatitis, but NAS was designed to measure change, not to diagnose MASH. Drug trials enrol 'at-risk MASH' (NAS ≥4 with ≥1 in each component and F2–F3). Endpoints are 'MASH resolution' (ballooning 0, inflammation 0–1) and '≥1-stage fibrosis improvement'. Inter-observer variability is a known problem, which has driven AI-based digital pathology tools.

attrs.mnemonic: NAS = 'S-I-B 3-3-2': Steatosis 3 + Inflammation 3 + Ballooning 2 = 8 points max.

items.gloss_md: Histological scoring system for chronic hepatitis C (Bedossa & Poynard, 1996) that grades necroinflammatory activity A0–A3 and stages fibrosis F0–F4.
items.body_md:
Fibrosis stages:

- F0: no fibrosis.
- F1: portal fibrosis without septa.
- F2: portal fibrosis with few septa.
- F3: numerous septa without cirrhosis.
- F4: cirrhosis.

Activity A0 (none) to A3 (severe), from piecemeal (interface) necrosis and lobular necrosis.

- The F0–F4 scale has become the common language of fibrosis everywhere ('F3 patient'). Non-invasive tests are calibrated against it.
- 'Significant fibrosis' F≥2, 'advanced fibrosis' F≥3.
- Designed for viral hepatitis. Steatotic liver disease uses NASH CRN (Kleiner) staging, which also runs from 0 to 4 but defines the early stages differently (zone 3 perisinusoidal fibrosis).

attrs.mnemonic: METAVIR F-stages: 'nothing – portal – a few septa – many septa – cirrhosis'.
attrs.anecdote: METAVIR is not a person: it is the French METAVIR cooperative study group, formed to pool histological data on viral hepatitis, whose pathologists created the score.

items.gloss_md: Commercial blood test (Siemens) that combines three direct matrix markers — hyaluronic acid, PIIINP and TIMP-1 — into a score that estimates liver fibrosis severity.
items.body_md:
- Components: hyaluronic acid (HA), amino-terminal propeptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP), tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases-1 (TIMP-1).
- Manufacturer bands: below 7.7 none/mild, 7.7 to below 9.8 moderate, 9.8 to below 11.3 severe, 11.3 or more cirrhosis.
- Common thresholds in MASLD pathways: below 7.7 to rule out, 9.8 or more for high risk of advanced fibrosis. NICE (UK) used ≥10.51 for advanced fibrosis in NAFLD.
- Used as the second step after an indeterminate FIB-4 when elastography is not available. Also prognostic for liver events.
- Influenced by age and extrahepatic fibrosis or inflammation (e.g. arthritis).

attrs.mnemonic: ELF = 'HA, P3, TIMP-1' — three matrix markers: hyaluronic acid (made), procollagen III (laid down), TIMP-1 (stops breakdown).

items.gloss_md: Steatosis measure (in dB/m) obtained with transient elastography from the attenuation of the ultrasound signal. Higher values mean more liver fat.
items.body_md:
- Range about 100–400 dB/m. Commonly ≥275 dB/m (EASL guidance) indicates steatosis. Cut-offs for grades S1–S3 vary between studies (roughly 250–300 dB/m).
- Less accurate for grading than MRI-PDFF, but cheap and point-of-care.
- Part of the FAST score (with LSM and AST) for identifying at-risk MASH.

- Values are influenced by BMI, diabetes and probe type (M vs XL). Results should be interpreted together with the IQR and the clinical context.
- In research cohorts, CAP is often used to define steatosis on a population scale (e.g. NHANES 2017–2020 used FibroScan), which is why prevalence estimates of MASLD differ with the chosen threshold.

attrs.mnemonic: CAP = 'Cap on fat': the dB/m tells you how much the fat dampens the ultrasound.

items.gloss_md: Non-invasive score for advanced fibrosis in NAFLD/MASLD from age, BMI, hyperglycaemia/diabetes, AST/ALT ratio, platelets and albumin.
items.body_md:
NFS = −1.675 + 0.037 × age + 0.094 × BMI + 1.13 × (impaired fasting glucose or diabetes: yes = 1) + 0.99 × AST/ALT − 0.013 × platelets (10⁹/L) − 0.66 × albumin (g/dL).

- Below −1.455: advanced fibrosis unlikely. Above 0.676: likely. In between: indeterminate.
- Developed by Angulo et al. (2007).
- Similar performance to FIB-4 but needs more variables. Many guidelines now prefer FIB-4 as the first step.

items.gloss_md: Simple fibrosis index: (AST/ULN) ÷ platelet count (10⁹/L) × 100. It was developed for chronic hepatitis C and is widely used in resource-limited settings.
items.body_md:
- Significant fibrosis: below 0.5 rules out, above 1.5 rules in. Cirrhosis: below 1.0 rules out, above 2.0 rules in (WHO HCV guidance).
- Developed by Wai et al. (2003) in HCV.
- Less accurate than FIB-4 in MASLD. Still used in HBV/HCV programmes and in research cohorts lacking ALT.

- Advantages: uses only routine labs and needs no age, ALT or calculator beyond a simple ratio. This made it a cornerstone of WHO HCV treatment guidance in settings without elastography.
- Disadvantages: platelets are affected by hypersplenism and other diseases, AST by muscle and alcohol, and the indeterminate zone is large.

attrs.mnemonic: APRI = 'AST Per Platelet'.

items.gloss_md: Histological system for chronic hepatitis (Ishak et al., 1995) with a necroinflammatory grade of 0–18 and a fibrosis stage of 0–6.
items.body_md:
- Fibrosis stages: 0 none; 1–2 portal fibrous expansion (some/most portal areas); 3–4 bridging fibrosis (occasional/marked); 5 incomplete cirrhosis; 6 cirrhosis.
- Finer resolution than METAVIR in advanced stages, so it is used in trials of chronic viral hepatitis and for measuring regression.
- Modified from Knodell's Histological Activity Index (HAI, 1981).

- The necroinflammatory grade sums interface hepatitis (0–4), confluent necrosis (0–6), focal lytic necrosis/apoptosis/focal inflammation (0–4) and portal inflammation (0–4).
- Ishak stages can be mapped approximately to METAVIR (e.g. Ishak 3–4 to F3, 5–6 to F4), but not exactly, which matters when comparing studies.

attrs.mnemonic: Ishak goes to 6 (METAVIR only to 4): Ishak 5 = 'almost cirrhosis', 6 = cirrhosis.

items.gloss_md: European histological scoring system for steatotic liver disease (Bedossa et al., 2012) with separate scores for Steatosis (S0–S3), Activity (A0–A4 = ballooning 0–2 + lobular inflammation 0–2) and Fibrosis (F0–F4).
items.body_md:
- The FLIP algorithm (Fatty Liver Inhibition of Progression consortium) uses steatosis, ballooning and inflammation to classify a biopsy as no MASLD, MASL, or MASH. Steatohepatitis requires steatosis ≥1, ballooning ≥1 and lobular inflammation ≥1.
- Separates activity from steatosis (unlike NAS, which adds them up), with better inter-observer agreement.
- Used in European cohorts such as LITMUS.

attrs.mnemonic: SAF spells its own content: Steatosis, Activity, Fibrosis.

items.gloss_md: MRI technique that images shear waves induced by an external driver to map liver stiffness across the whole liver. It is the most accurate non-invasive stiffness method and is often used in MASH trials together with MRI-PDFF.
items.body_md:
- Less sampling error than transient elastography (whole-liver maps), works in obesity and ascites.
- Expensive, limited availability, fails with iron overload (gradient-echo sequences).
- Cut-offs around 3.6 kPa for advanced fibrosis are commonly cited (note: MRE kPa values are not comparable with FibroScan kPa).
- Other shear-wave methods: point SWE (ARFI) and 2D-SWE built into conventional ultrasound machines.

items.gloss_md: First systematic grading (1–3) and staging (1–4) system for NASH histology, proposed by Elizabeth Brunt in 1999. It was the precursor of the NASH CRN/NAS system.
items.body_md:
- Grade: mild, moderate, severe activity (steatosis, ballooning, inflammation).
- Stage: 1 zone 3 perisinusoidal fibrosis; 2 + portal fibrosis; 3 bridging; 4 cirrhosis.
- Brunt later co-led the NASH CRN, whose Kleiner/NAS score refined this framework. Older papers report Brunt stages.

- Developed from biopsies of patients with NASH and published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology.
- It established the pattern that steatohepatitis starts in zone 3 with perisinusoidal 'chicken-wire' fibrosis, unlike the portal-based fibrosis of viral hepatitis. Both METAVIR and NASH CRN staging reach 4 = cirrhosis, but their early stages are not interchangeable, which matters when merging datasets from different eras.

items.gloss_md: Fetal serum glycoprotein (gene AFP, 4q13) that is re-expressed by many HCCs. It serves as a tumour marker for HCC surveillance, diagnosis support and prognosis, and in transplant selection.
items.body_md:
- Normal adult level below about 10–20 ng/mL. Raised in HCC (sensitivity only about 60% in early HCC), also in germ-cell tumours (yolk-sac), pregnancy and active hepatitis/regeneration.
- AFP ≥400 ng/mL is a poor prognostic factor and an inclusion criterion for ramucirumab (REACH-2).
- In transplantation, AFP above 1000 ng/mL indicates high recurrence risk and is used as an exclusion threshold in several selection models (e.g. French AFP model, US UNOS policy).
- AFP-L3 (lectin-reactive fraction) and DCP/PIVKA-II improve detection. GALAD combines Gender, Age, AFP-L3, AFP and DCP.

attrs.mnemonic: '400 bad, 1000 too bad for transplant.'
attrs.anecdote: AFP was the first oncofetal protein used as a tumour marker. Garri Abelev in Moscow showed in 1963 that mouse hepatomas produce it, and Yuri Tatarinov found it in the serum of human HCC patients in 1964.

items.gloss_md: Regular screening of high-risk patients (cirrhosis, certain HBV carriers) with liver ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months to detect HCC at a curable stage.
items.body_md:
- Target groups: all cirrhosis patients who would be treatment candidates (Child A/B; Child C only if listed for transplant); non-cirrhotic HBV with high PAGE-B or family history; F3 fibrosis is considered in some guidelines; HCV-cured cirrhosis remains in surveillance.
- 6-month interval based on tumour doubling time. Detection of early-stage HCC improves survival in observational data.
- Abdominal ultrasound often fails in obesity/MASLD. Abbreviated MRI and biomarker panels (GALAD) are being evaluated.

items.label_md: Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS)
items.gloss_md: American College of Radiology system that standardises CT/MRI (and CEUS) reporting of liver observations in patients at high risk of HCC, classifying them from LR-1 (definitely benign) to LR-5 (definitely HCC).
items.body_md:
- Categories: LR-1 definitely benign; LR-2 probably benign; LR-3 intermediate; LR-4 probably HCC; LR-5 definitely HCC; LR-M probably/definitely malignant but not HCC-specific (e.g. cholangiocarcinoma); LR-TIV tumour in vein; LR-NC not categorisable.
- Major features: non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (APHE), non-peripheral washout, enhancing 'capsule', size, threshold growth (≥50% in ≤6 months).
- Example: LR-5 = APHE with size ≥20 mm and at least one additional major feature (or 10–19 mm with washout or threshold growth).
- Valid only in high-risk populations (cirrhosis, chronic HBV, current/prior HCC). Not for non-cirrhotic MASLD without HBV.
- LR-5 allows diagnosis of HCC without biopsy and is accepted for transplant listing (OPTN class 5 is a related US system). The core CT/MRI version is v2018.

attrs.mnemonic: Like BI-RADS for the breast: 1 = benign, 5 = cancer. 'LR-M = Malignant, but Maybe not HCC.'

items.gloss_md: Adenocarcinoma of the bile duct epithelium, classified as intrahepatic (iCCA), perihilar (pCCA, Klatskin tumour) or distal (dCCA). It has a poor prognosis, and iCCA has many targetable alterations.
items.body_md:
- Risk factors: PSC, liver flukes (Opisthorchis, Clonorchis), choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis, cirrhosis, HBV/HCV, MASLD. Most cases are sporadic.
- Perihilar tumours are graded by Bismuth–Corlette (types I–IV by ductal extent).
- Marker: CA 19-9 (also raised in cholestasis and PDAC).
- Molecular (mainly iCCA): FGFR2 fusions (about 10–15%; pemigatinib, futibatinib), IDH1 mutations (about 13%; ivosidenib), BRAF V600E, HER2, NTRK, MSI-high. Molecular profiling is recommended.
- Treatment: resection is the only cure (minority resectable); adjuvant capecitabine. Advanced first line: gemcitabine + cisplatin + durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) or pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-966).
- Liver transplantation for unresectable early perihilar CCA after neoadjuvant chemoradiation (Mayo protocol) in selected centres. Transplant for iCCA is under study.

attrs.anecdote: Gerald Klatskin of Yale described perihilar bile duct tumours in 1965, hence the 'Klatskin tumour'. In German hospitals 'Klatskin-Tumor' remains everyday vocabulary.

items.gloss_md: Expanded HCC transplant criteria: the sum of the diameter of the largest tumour (cm) and the number of tumours must not exceed 7, without microvascular invasion. Patients within these limits but beyond Milan had similar survival.
items.body_md:
- Proposed by Mazzaferro et al. (Lancet Oncology 2009), from the 'Metroticket' study of over 1500 patients.
- Example: 3 tumours with the largest 4 cm (3 + 4 = 7) is within up-to-seven but beyond Milan.
- Microvascular invasion is only known on explant histology, which limits use before transplantation.
- Also used to subdivide BCLC B (intermediate) HCC: 'within up-to-seven' patients do better with TACE.
- Metroticket 2.0 extended the concept with AFP.

attrs.mnemonic: Number + biggest size ≤ 7 — 'Milan in your pocket, seven in your hand'.

items.gloss_md: Objective liver-function score built only from albumin and bilirubin, used mainly in HCC to grade liver function without subjective clinical parameters.
items.body_md:
ALBI = 0.66 × log₁₀(bilirubin, µmol/L) − 0.085 × albumin (g/L).

- Grade 1: ≤ −2.60; grade 2: > −2.60 to ≤ −1.39; grade 3: > −1.39.
- Separates Child-Pugh A patients into prognostic subgroups. Used in the BCLC 2022 update and in HCC trials. Grade 2 is often split into 2a/2b (mALBI).
- Developed by Johnson et al. (2015) in international HCC cohorts.

items.gloss_md: Transplant selection score for HCC (Duvoux et al., 2012) that combines largest tumour diameter, tumour number and AFP. A score ≤2 predicts low recurrence risk even beyond Milan.
items.body_md:
- Largest diameter: ≤3 cm = 0, 3–6 cm = 1, >6 cm = 4.
- Number of nodules: 1–3 = 0, ≥4 = 2.
- AFP: ≤100 ng/mL = 0, 100–1000 = 2, >1000 = 3.
- ≤2 points: low risk. Over 2: high risk.
- Adopted for transplant eligibility in France. Illustrates the shift from pure morphology to biology (AFP) in HCC transplant selection.

items.gloss_md: Expanded HCC transplant criteria from the University of California San Francisco (Yao et al., 2001): a single tumour ≤6.5 cm, or ≤3 tumours with the largest ≤4.5 cm and total diameter ≤8 cm, without vascular invasion.
items.body_md:
- Showed survival comparable to Milan in selected patients slightly beyond Milan.
- Basis of the US UNOS downstaging protocol (patients downstaged from beyond Milan but within 'UCSF-downstaging' limits).

- Patients beyond Milan but within UCSF had post-transplant survival comparable to Milan in the original and later validation series, although recurrence risk is somewhat higher.
- UCSF, up-to-seven and AFP-based models are examples of the 'expanded criteria' debate: balancing the benefit for the individual patient against the use of scarce organs that could save others on the waiting list.
- In Eurotransplant/Germany, standard exception points are tied to the Milan criteria, not to UCSF.

items.gloss_md: First-line systemic therapy for advanced or unresectable HCC: the anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab with the anti-VEGF-A antibody bevacizumab, which improved overall survival over sorafenib in the IMbrave150 trial.
items.body_md:
- IMbrave150 (Finn et al., NEJM 2020): hazard ratio for death 0.58 at the first analysis. Median OS about 19 months versus 13 months for sorafenib in the updated analysis.
- Dosing: atezolizumab 1200 mg + bevacizumab 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks.
- Requires Child-Pugh A and controlled bleeding risk: varices must be screened by endoscopy (within 6 months) and treated before starting, because bevacizumab raises bleeding risk.
- Side effects: hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, immune-related adverse events (hepatitis, thyroiditis, colitis).
- Caution after liver transplantation: immune checkpoint inhibitors can trigger fatal graft rejection.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Atezo blocks the brake (PD-L1), Bev starves the vessels (VEGF)': immunotherapy plus anti-angiogenesis.

items.gloss_md: Catheter-based treatment that delivers chemotherapy (e.g. doxorubicin with lipiodol, or drug-eluting beads) into the arteries feeding an HCC and then embolises them. It is the standard treatment for intermediate-stage (BCLC B) HCC.
items.body_md:
- Rationale: HCC is supplied mainly by the hepatic artery, the normal liver mainly by the portal vein.
- Variants: conventional TACE (cTACE, lipiodol emulsion + chemotherapy + embolic particles) and DEB-TACE (drug-eluting beads). Bland embolisation (TAE) without chemotherapy.
- Survival benefit over supportive care shown in randomised trials around 2002 (Llovet et al.; Lo et al.).
- Contraindications: decompensated cirrhosis, main portal vein tumour thrombosis, severe arterioportal shunting, renal failure.
- Post-embolisation syndrome (fever, pain, nausea) is common.
- Uses: BCLC B, bridging or downstaging to transplant. Response assessed by mRECIST. Combinations with systemic therapy (e.g. EMERALD-1, LEAP-012) are being studied.

attrs.mnemonic: TACE = 'Throttle the Artery, Chemo Enters'.

items.gloss_md: First-line systemic therapy for advanced HCC: a single priming dose of the anti-CTLA-4 antibody tremelimumab plus the anti-PD-L1 antibody durvalumab every 4 weeks (STRIDE regimen), which improved survival over sorafenib in HIMALAYA.
items.body_md:
- STRIDE = Single Tremelimumab Regular Interval Durvalumab: tremelimumab 300 mg once + durvalumab 1500 mg, then durvalumab every 4 weeks.
- HIMALAYA trial (Abou-Alfa et al., NEJM Evidence 2022): OS benefit vs sorafenib, with a durable long-term survival tail (about 20% alive at 5 years in follow-up).
- No VEGF component, so it is an option for patients with high bleeding risk or untreated varices.
- Immune-related adverse events. Contraindicated after transplantation (rejection).
- Nivolumab + ipilimumab (CheckMate 9DW) is another dual checkpoint first-line option.

attrs.mnemonic: STRIDE: one big step with tremelimumab, then regular strides with durvalumab.

items.gloss_md: Surgical removal of the tumour-bearing liver segments. It is first-line curative treatment for single HCC in patients with preserved liver function, no clinically significant portal hypertension and an adequate future liver remnant.
items.body_md:
- Candidates: non-cirrhotic liver, or Child-Pugh A without CSPH (HVPG below 10 mmHg). Normal bilirubin. Adequate future liver remnant (FLR): usually ≥20–25% in a normal liver, ≥40% in cirrhosis. Portal vein embolisation can grow the FLR before surgery.
- Anatomical resection follows Couinaud segments. Laparoscopic or robotic approaches reduce morbidity.
- Main risk: post-hepatectomy liver failure (ISGLS criteria; 50-50 rule: PT <50% and bilirubin >50 µmol/L on day 5).
- Recurrence in the remnant liver is about 70% at 5 years (de novo and metastatic). Salvage transplantation is possible.

attrs.mnemonic: Resection in cirrhosis: 'A without pressure' — Child A and no CSPH.

items.gloss_md: Oral multikinase inhibitor (VEGFR, PDGFR, RAF). It was the first systemic drug to prolong survival in advanced HCC (SHARP trial, 2008) and is now mostly used when immunotherapy is unsuitable.
items.body_md:
- SHARP (Llovet et al., NEJM 2008): median OS 10.7 vs 7.9 months against placebo.
- Trade name Nexavar. Dose 400 mg twice daily.
- Side effects: hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhoea, fatigue, hypertension.
- Was the comparator arm in most later first-line trials (IMbrave150, HIMALAYA, REFLECT). Also used for HCC recurrence after liver transplantation, where checkpoint inhibitors carry rejection risk.
- Also approved for renal cell and thyroid cancer.

attrs.mnemonic: Sorafenib: 'SO RAF', it blocks RAF (and VEGFR); in SHARP it gave HCC its first sharp win.

items.gloss_md: Percutaneous destruction of a tumour by heat, using radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or microwave ablation (MWA). It is curative first-line treatment for very early HCC (≤2–3 cm), with results comparable to resection.
items.body_md:
- Image-guided needle electrodes create a coagulation zone with a safety margin of about 5–10 mm.
- Best for tumours ≤3 cm and away from large vessels (heat-sink effect, less with MWA), bile ducts and bowel.
- Alternatives: percutaneous ethanol injection (historical), irreversible electroporation, cryoablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT).
- Also used as a 'bridge' to transplantation and for downstaging.

items.gloss_md: Oral multikinase inhibitor (VEGFR1–3, FGFR1–4, PDGFRα, RET, KIT) approved for first-line treatment of advanced HCC after it proved non-inferior to sorafenib in the REFLECT trial (2018).
items.body_md:
- REFLECT (Kudo et al., Lancet 2018): median OS 13.6 vs 12.3 months (non-inferior), with higher response rate.
- Trade name Lenvima. Weight-based dosing (8 or 12 mg/day).
- Side effects: hypertension, proteinuria, fatigue, hypothyroidism, decreased appetite.
- Used when checkpoint inhibitors are contraindicated (e.g. after liver transplant, autoimmune disease) and as second line after immunotherapy (off-label, common practice).
- Later lines in HCC: regorafenib (RESORCE, after sorafenib), cabozantinib (CELESTIAL), ramucirumab for AFP ≥400 ng/mL (REACH-2).

items.gloss_md: Transarterial radioembolisation: yttrium-90 (⁹⁰Y)-loaded glass or resin microspheres are injected into the hepatic arteries supplying the tumour, delivering high-dose β-radiation locally.
items.body_md:
- ⁹⁰Y is a pure β-emitter (half-life about 64 h, tissue penetration a few mm).
- Preparatory angiography with ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA scintigraphy estimates lung shunt and blocks extrahepatic vessels (e.g. gastroduodenal artery) to avoid radiation pneumonitis or gastric ulcers.
- Can be used in segmental portal vein thrombosis, unlike TACE.
- Trials against sorafenib in advanced HCC (SARAH, SIRveNIB) showed no survival benefit, but better tolerability.
- 'Radiation segmentectomy' at high dose can be curative for early single HCC (LEGACY study). Also used for bridging and downstaging. Radioembolisation-induced liver disease (REILD) is a complication.

items.gloss_md: Infection with the hepatitis B virus, a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus. Chronic infection affects roughly 250–300 million people worldwide and causes cirrhosis and HCC, which can occur even without cirrhosis.
items.body_md:
- The virus persists as cccDNA in hepatocyte nuclei and integrates into the host genome, which is why HBsAg loss ('functional cure') is rare.
- Serology: HBsAg (infection); anti-HBc (contact ever; IgM = acute); anti-HBs (immunity: vaccine alone, or with anti-HBc after recovery); HBeAg/anti-HBe; HBV DNA (viral load).
- Chronicity: about 90% after perinatal infection, about 5% or less after adult infection.
- EASL phases: HBeAg-positive chronic infection or hepatitis; HBeAg-negative chronic infection or hepatitis; HBsAg-negative phase (occult infection).
- Treatment: nucleos(t)ide analogues (entecavir, tenofovir DF/AF), usually long-term; pegylated interferon-α for selected patients.
- HCC risk scores: PAGE-B.
- Reactivation risk under immunosuppression (rituximab, chemotherapy, transplantation), so test before such therapy and give prophylaxis.
- After liver transplantation for HBV: HBIG plus a nucleos(t)ide analogue prevents recurrence.
- Effective vaccine (since the 1980s, recombinant). HDV coinfection requires HBsAg.

attrs.mnemonic: Serology 'S-C-S': HBsAg = Sick now, anti-HBc = Contact ever, anti-HBs = Shielded (immune).
attrs.anecdote: Baruch Blumberg discovered the 'Australia antigen' (later shown to be HBsAg) in the blood of an Aboriginal Australian in the 1960s while studying blood polymorphisms. He received the 1976 Nobel Prize, and the HBV vaccine became the first vaccine against a cancer (HCC).

items.gloss_md: Infection with the hepatitis C virus, a positive-strand RNA virus (Hepacivirus, Flaviviridae) transmitted by blood. Most infections become chronic, and the disease is now curable in over 95% with direct-acting antivirals.
items.body_md:
- Transmission: injection drug use, unsafe medical procedures, historically blood products before screening (1990s).
- About two-thirds or more of infected people develop chronic infection, which can progress over decades to cirrhosis and HCC.
- Diagnosis: anti-HCV screening, then confirmation by HCV RNA (PCR). Several genotypes (1–8; genotype 3 is associated with steatosis and faster progression).
- Treatment: pangenotypic DAAs for 8–12 weeks, e.g. sofosbuvir/velpatasvir or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Cure is defined as SVR12 (undetectable RNA 12 weeks after treatment). There is no vaccine.
- Before DAAs, HCV cirrhosis was a leading indication for liver transplantation, and recurrence in the graft was universal and aggressive. Today it has declined dramatically, and HCV-positive donor organs can be used in negative recipients with DAA treatment.
- HCC risk persists after cure if cirrhosis was present, so surveillance must continue.

attrs.anecdote: HCV was identified in 1989 by Michael Houghton's group (Chiron) by molecular cloning, without ever growing the virus. Houghton, Harvey Alter and Charles Rice received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

items.gloss_md: Oral drugs that inhibit HCV proteins (NS3/4A protease, NS5A, NS5B polymerase). Combinations cure over 95% of patients in 8–12 weeks and have replaced interferon-based therapy.
items.body_md:
- Classes: NS5B polymerase inhibitors (sofosbuvir, nucleotide analogue); NS5A inhibitors (velpatasvir, ledipasvir, pibrentasvir); NS3/4A protease inhibitors (glecaprevir, voxilaprevir, grazoprevir).
- Pangenotypic regimens: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa, 12 weeks), glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Maviret, 8 weeks). Retreatment: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (Vosevi).
- Protease inhibitors are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis (Child B/C).
- Drug–drug interactions matter, including with tacrolimus and ciclosporin after transplantation.
- Effect on transplantation: HCV is no longer a major indication. HCV-viraemic donor organs (also hearts, kidneys, lungs) can be given to negative recipients with DAA treatment afterwards.
- WHO goal: eliminate HCV as a public health threat by 2030.

attrs.anecdote: When sofosbuvir launched in the US in 2013, its price of about 1000 US dollars per pill (84,000 dollars per course) triggered a worldwide debate on drug pricing and a US Senate investigation.

items.gloss_md: Rapid loss of liver function (INR ≥1.5 and hepatic encephalopathy) within 26 weeks in a patient without pre-existing liver disease. It is a rare emergency with high mortality that often requires high-urgency liver transplantation.
items.body_md:
- O'Grady subtypes by jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval: hyperacute (≤7 days; e.g. paracetamol, HAV/HEV; cerebral oedema common but best spontaneous survival), acute (8–28 days), subacute (5–12 weeks; worst spontaneous survival).
- Causes: paracetamol, idiosyncratic DILI, viral (HBV, HAV, HEV, HSV), AIH, Wilson disease, Budd–Chiari, ischaemic hepatitis, pregnancy-related (HELLP, acute fatty liver), mushroom (Amanita phalloides) poisoning; many are indeterminate.
- Treatment: ICU care, N-acetylcysteine (also beneficial in non-paracetamol ALF), management of cerebral oedema (ammonia, sodium), infection control, transfer to a transplant centre.
- King's College criteria (paracetamol): arterial pH below 7.3 after resuscitation, or all of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 300 µmol/L and HE grade 3–4. Patients meeting criteria are listed as high urgency (HU) with Eurotransplant.

attrs.mnemonic: ALF = 'INR ≥1.5 + HE + no prior liver disease + <26 weeks'.

items.gloss_md: Chronic immune-mediated hepatitis with interface hepatitis, raised IgG and autoantibodies. It mostly affects women, responds well to immunosuppression, and progresses to cirrhosis if untreated.
items.body_md:
- Types: type 1 (ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies, SMA/anti-actin; also anti-SLA/LP), mostly adults; type 2 (anti-LKM-1, anti-LC1), mostly children.
- Presentation: from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to acute hepatitis and acute liver failure.
- Diagnosis: simplified IAIHG criteria (Hennes et al. 2008: autoantibodies, IgG, histology, exclusion of viral hepatitis). Biopsy is required: interface hepatitis, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, rosettes, emperipolesis.
- Treatment: prednisolone (or budesonide in non-cirrhotic patients) plus azathioprine (TPMT check). Mycophenolate is second-line. Treatment is usually long-term, and relapse after withdrawal is common.
- Overlap syndromes with PBC or PSC exist.
- Recurs after liver transplantation, and de novo AIH can arise in grafts transplanted for other indications.

attrs.mnemonic: Type 1 = ANA + SMA (adults); type 2 = LKM-1 (kids). 'IgG high, interface on fire, steroids put it out.'

items.gloss_md: Chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease with destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, characterised by antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA). About 90% of patients are women, typically middle-aged.
items.body_md:
- Formerly 'primary biliary cirrhosis'. Renamed in 2015 because most patients never develop cirrhosis.
- Diagnosis: chronically raised ALP + AMA (anti-PDC-E2, the M2 antigen; positive in about 95%) or PBC-specific ANA (anti-gp210, anti-sp100). A biopsy is usually unnecessary (florid duct lesion, granulomatous cholangitis).
- Symptoms: fatigue, pruritus, sicca. Associated with Sjögren syndrome and thyroid disease. Raised IgM.
- First-line treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, 13–15 mg/kg/day), which normalises life expectancy in responders. Response is assessed after 12 months (Paris II, POISE criteria; GLOBE or UK-PBC risk scores).
- Second-line: PPAR agonists elafibranor and seladelpar (approved 2024), bezafibrate off-label. Obeticholic acid (FXR agonist) lost its EU authorisation in 2024.
- Pruritus: cholestyramine, bezafibrate, IBAT inhibitors in trials.
- Liver transplantation for end stage. The disease recurs in the graft in a substantial minority.

attrs.mnemonic: PBC = 'Primarily Bothers Women, Cholestasis with AMA'. M2 for the 'mitochondrial' antibody.

items.gloss_md: Chronic progressive cholestatic disease with inflammation and multifocal strictures of intra- and/or extrahepatic bile ducts. It is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (mostly ulcerative colitis) and carries a high cancer risk.
items.body_md:
- Mostly men (about 2:1), median age at diagnosis about 40. About 60–80% of Northern European patients have IBD.
- Diagnosis: cholestatic enzymes + MRCP showing a 'beaded' pattern of strictures and dilatations. Small-duct PSC needs a biopsy. Atypical p-ANCA is common but not specific. Exclude IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and secondary causes.
- Complications: bacterial cholangitis, dominant strictures, cirrhosis, cholangiocarcinoma (markedly increased risk), gallbladder carcinoma, colorectal cancer in PSC-IBD (yearly colonoscopy).
- No proven medical therapy that changes survival. UDCA is used in moderate dose in some countries, not high-dose (harm in a trial). Endoscopic dilatation of dominant strictures.
- Liver transplantation is the only curative therapy. PSC recurs in the graft in a substantial minority (often cited around 20%).

attrs.mnemonic: PSC = 'Perlschnur, Sklerose, Colitis' (de): string-of-pearls bile ducts, sclerosing scars and ulcerative colitis. Opposite of PBC: men, large ducts, no AMA.
attrs.anecdote: Walter Payton, the American football star nicknamed 'Sweetness', made PSC widely known when he went public in 1999 about needing a liver transplant. He died of cholangiocarcinoma before he could receive one.

items.gloss_md: Liver injury caused by drugs, herbal or dietary supplements. It is either intrinsic (dose-dependent, predictable, e.g. paracetamol) or idiosyncratic (rare, unpredictable, e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate), and is a leading cause of acute liver failure and drug withdrawal.
items.body_md:
- Intrinsic: paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the UK and US. The toxic metabolite NAPQI depletes glutathione. Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (Rumack–Matthew nomogram).
- Idiosyncratic: amoxicillin-clavulanate (most common in Western series), isoniazid, NSAIDs (diclofenac), antiepileptics, checkpoint inhibitors (immune-mediated hepatitis), green tea extract, anabolic steroids. HLA associations exist (e.g. HLA-B*57:01 with flucloxacillin).
- Patterns: hepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed (R ratio).
- Causality: RUCAM, or the newer RECAM.
- Severity: Hy's law cases carry about 10% risk of death or transplantation.
- Management: stop the drug; steroids for immune-mediated forms; transplant evaluation in ALF.

items.label_md: Nucleos(t)ide analogues for hepatitis B (entecavir, tenofovir)
items.gloss_md: Oral antivirals that inhibit HBV reverse transcriptase and suppress HBV DNA. They are first-line, usually long-term, treatment for chronic hepatitis B and HBV prophylaxis in transplantation and immunosuppression.
items.body_md:
- First-line drugs with high resistance barrier: entecavir (ETV), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), tenofovir alafenamide (TAF, less renal/bone toxicity). Lamivudine and adefovir are outdated (resistance).
- Suppress replication but do not eliminate cccDNA. HBsAg loss is rare, so therapy is usually indefinite. Stopping can cause flares.
- Reduce progression, HCC risk and decompensation. Can lead to fibrosis regression.
- After liver transplantation for HBV: nucleos(t)ide analogue lifelong ± hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) prevents graft reinfection.
- Prophylaxis during rituximab, chemotherapy and in recipients of anti-HBc-positive donor livers.

items.gloss_md: Inherited iron overload caused by inadequate hepcidin, most commonly homozygosity for the HFE C282Y variant. Iron accumulates in liver, heart, pancreas, joints and skin.
items.body_md:
- HFE type 1, autosomal recessive. C282Y homozygosity occurs in about 1 in 200–300 Northern Europeans, but penetrance (clinical disease) is incomplete and higher in men. Rare non-HFE forms involve HJV, HAMP, TFR2 and SLC40A1.
- Mechanism: low hepcidin, so ferroportin stays active, causing high intestinal iron uptake and macrophage release.
- Diagnosis: transferrin saturation above 45% + raised ferritin, then HFE genotyping. MRI (T2*) quantifies liver iron. Biopsy if ferritin is above 1000 µg/L or enzymes are raised (to check for cirrhosis).
- Clinical picture: fatigue, arthropathy (second and third MCP joints), liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, HCC, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism, skin pigmentation ('bronze diabetes').
- Treatment: venesection (phlebotomy), initially weekly, to a ferritin of about 50–100 µg/L, then maintenance.
- Note: raised ferritin alone is far more often due to MASLD, alcohol or inflammation (dysmetabolic hyperferritinaemia).

attrs.mnemonic: 'C282Y — the Celtic curse': a Northern European founder mutation. Remember the trio 'transferrin saturation >45, ferritin high, phlebotomy'.
attrs.anecdote: The disease was nicknamed 'bronze diabetes' in 19th-century France, and the HFE mutation is so common in people of Irish descent that it is popularly called the 'Celtic curse'.

items.gloss_md: Hydrophilic bile acid that is first-line therapy for primary biliary cholangitis (13–15 mg/kg/day). It improves biochemistry and transplant-free survival in responders.
items.body_md:
- Mechanisms: replaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids, stimulates biliary secretion (bicarbonate umbrella), is cytoprotective and anti-apoptotic.
- Response assessed after 12 months (Paris I/II, Barcelona, Toronto, POISE criteria; GLOBE and UK-PBC continuous scores). About 30–40% respond inadequately and need second-line therapy: PPAR agonists elafibranor (Iqirvo) or seladelpar (Livdelzi), both approved 2024; bezafibrate off-label. Obeticholic acid (Ocaliva, FXR agonist) lost its EU authorisation in 2024.
- Other uses: gallstone dissolution, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, prophylaxis of PBC recurrence after liver transplantation. In PSC, high doses were harmful, and moderate doses are debated.

attrs.anecdote: Ursodeoxycholic acid takes its name from bears (Latin ursus). Bear bile, rich in UDCA, has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries; UDCA was first characterised from bear bile in Japan in the 1920s–1930s.

items.gloss_md: Autosomal recessive copper-storage disorder caused by mutations in ATP7B (13q14). It leads to copper accumulation in liver and brain, with hepatic, neurological or psychiatric disease, usually before age 40.
items.body_md:
- ATP7B is a copper-transporting ATPase that loads copper into ceruloplasmin and excretes it into bile. In Wilson disease, ceruloplasmin is low and free copper accumulates.
- Presentations: hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure (often young women, with Coombs-negative haemolysis, very low ALP, ALP/bilirubin ratio below 4); neurological (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria) and psychiatric symptoms; Kayser–Fleischer rings on the cornea.
- Diagnosis: low ceruloplasmin, raised 24-h urinary copper, hepatic copper content above 250 µg/g dry weight, genetics. The Leipzig score combines these.
- Treatment: chelators (D-penicillamine, trientine) or zinc (blocks intestinal absorption), lifelong.
- Fulminant Wilson disease is an indication for urgent (high-urgency) liver transplantation, which corrects the defect.

attrs.mnemonic: Wilson = copper 'will stay on': can't excrete it. Look for 'K-F rings' (Kayser–Fleischer) and low ceruloplasmin; ATP7B on chromosome 13 = 'unlucky copper'.
attrs.anecdote: Samuel Alexander Kinnier Wilson described 'progressive lenticular degeneration' with liver cirrhosis in his 1912 thesis in London.

items.gloss_md: Inherited deficiency of the serine protease inhibitor α1-antitrypsin, caused by SERPINA1 variants (mainly PiZZ). Misfolded protein retained in hepatocytes causes liver disease, and lack of circulating protein causes emphysema.
items.body_md:
- SERPINA1 on 14q32. Alleles: M (normal), Z (Glu342Lys, severe), S (mild). PiZZ affects about 1 in 2000–5000 Europeans. PiMZ heterozygotes have a modestly raised risk of liver disease, especially with MASLD or alcohol.
- Liver: Z protein polymerises in the endoplasmic reticulum (gain-of-toxic-function). PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes. Neonatal cholestasis, later fibrosis/cirrhosis and HCC.
- Lung: protease–antiprotease imbalance (neutrophil elastase) causes panacinar basal emphysema, worse with smoking (loss of function).
- Diagnosis: low serum AAT, phenotyping/genotyping.
- Treatment: no smoking; IV augmentation therapy helps the lung but not the liver. Liver transplantation cures the liver disease (graft produces normal AAT). RNAi drugs (e.g. fazirsiran) that silence Z-AAT production are in trials.

attrs.mnemonic: Z for 'Zero function, Zone 1 globules': PiZZ hurts the liver by too much retained protein and the lung by too little circulating protein.

items.gloss_md: Infection with the hepatitis delta virus, a small defective RNA satellite virus that needs HBsAg from HBV for its envelope. It causes the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis.
items.body_md:
- Occurs only in HBsAg-positive people: as coinfection with acute HBV or as superinfection of chronic HBV carriers (usually becomes chronic).
- Rapid progression to cirrhosis and HCC.
- Screen every HBsAg-positive person with anti-HDV, then HDV RNA.
- Treatment: bulevirtide (Hepcludex), an entry inhibitor that blocks the bile-acid transporter NTCP (SLC10A1), the receptor used by HBV and HDV. Pegylated interferon-α is the alternative.
- Endemic regions: Mongolia, Central Asia, Eastern Europe, the Mediterranean, the Amazon basin. In Germany it is seen mostly in migrants.

attrs.mnemonic: Delta Depends on B: no HBsAg coat, no D.
attrs.anecdote: The delta antigen was discovered by Mario Rizzetto in Turin in 1977. It was first thought to be a new antigen of HBV itself.

items.gloss_md: Infection with the hepatitis E virus, an RNA virus. In Europe it is mainly a zoonosis (genotype 3, undercooked pork and game) and can become chronic in immunosuppressed transplant recipients.
items.body_md:
- Genotypes 1/2: waterborne epidemics in Asia/Africa, severe in pregnancy. Genotypes 3/4: zoonotic (pigs, wild boar, deer), the main type in Germany. Most infections are asymptomatic.
- Transplant recipients: chronic HEV infection (persistent RNA over 3 months) can cause rapid fibrosis. HEV must be included in the differential of raised liver enzymes after transplantation. Antibodies may be negative, so test HEV RNA (PCR).
- Treatment of chronic HEV: reduce immunosuppression; ribavirin for about 3 months.
- Extrahepatic manifestations: neuralgic amyotrophy, Guillain–Barré syndrome.
- HEV RNA screening of blood donations was introduced in Germany in 2020.

attrs.mnemonic: E = 'Eats' (pork) in Europe and 'Enteric' in the tropics; in transplant recipients E can become 'Eternal' (chronic).

items.gloss_md: Rule from drug development that hepatocellular injury with jaundice (ALT over 3× ULN plus bilirubin over 2× ULN, without initial cholestasis or another cause) signals a drug that can cause fatal liver injury, with about 10% mortality in such cases.
items.body_md:
- Criteria: ALT or AST over 3× ULN; total bilirubin over 2× ULN; ALP below 2× ULN (not primarily cholestatic); no other explanation (viral hepatitis, obstruction, other drugs).
- Used by FDA guidance and pharmacovigilance. Even a few Hy's law cases in a clinical trial raise major safety concerns.
- The eDISH plot (peak ALT vs peak bilirubin, log scale) visualises potential Hy's law cases in trial data, a common task for biostatisticians.

attrs.anecdote: Named after Hyman ('Hy') Zimmerman, the American hepatologist who observed in the 1970s that drug-induced hepatocellular jaundice carried a mortality of about 10–50%. The name 'Hy's law' was coined later by FDA staff.

items.gloss_md: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (hepatic veins or suprahepatic IVC), usually by thrombosis, causing congestive hepatopathy, ascites and portal hypertension.
items.body_md:
- Underlying cause in most patients: myeloproliferative neoplasms (JAK2 V617F, CALR), thrombophilia, oral contraceptives, PNH.
- Classic triad: abdominal pain, ascites, hepatomegaly. Caudate lobe hypertrophy (separate drainage into the IVC).
- Stepwise treatment: anticoagulation, angioplasty/stenting, TIPS, liver transplantation.

- Presentation ranges from fulminant liver failure to chronic portal hypertension. It can be asymptomatic when collaterals develop.
- Doppler ultrasound shows absent or reversed flow in hepatic veins and intrahepatic collaterals. CT/MRI confirm the diagnosis and show a 'nutmeg' perfusion pattern.
- Must be distinguished from sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), which affects the small sinusoidal vessels, for example after HSCT conditioning or oxaliplatin.

items.gloss_md: Non-profit organisation in Leiden (Netherlands) that allocates deceased-donor organs among eight member countries: Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Germany, Hungary, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Slovenia.
items.body_md:
- Founded in 1967 by the immunologist Jon van Rood, originally to allocate kidneys by HLA matching across a larger donor pool.
- Serves roughly 135–140 million inhabitants. Germany is by far the largest member and a net importer of organs.
- Allocation programmes: ETKAS (kidney), ESP (Eurotransplant Senior Program), ELAS (liver, MELD-based), EThAS (heart), lung (LAS in Germany), pancreas. Also the Acceptable Mismatch programme for highly sensitised kidney patients.
- Patients are registered by their transplant centre. The ET duty desk makes offers in the order of the match list, and centres accept or decline.
- National rules differ (e.g. donation laws, DCD allowed in the Netherlands, Belgium and Austria, but not in Germany). Balance between countries is managed by exchange rules.

attrs.mnemonic: Eight members, 'BeNeLux + DACH (minus CH) + HU, HR, SI': Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia.
attrs.anecdote: Jon van Rood, a Dutch immunologist and one of the discoverers of HLA, founded Eurotransplant in 1967 with the idea that a bigger pool would allow better HLA-matched kidneys for each recipient.

items.gloss_md: Organ donation from a deceased donor declared dead by neurological criteria while circulation is maintained by ventilation, so organs are perfused until procurement. In Germany it is the only form of deceased donation.
items.body_md:
- Advantages: no donor warm ischaemia, which gives better graft quality than DCD for the liver (fewer ischaemic biliary complications), heart and pancreas.
- Brain death itself harms organs (catecholamine storm, inflammation, hormonal failure), so donor management includes fluids, vasopressors, hormone therapy and lung-protective ventilation.
- Multi-organ procurement with cold flush (UW, HTK) and static cold storage or machine perfusion.
- Donor quality is described as standard or extended criteria (ECD): older age, steatosis, long ICU stay, high sodium, infections, malignancy history.

attrs.mnemonic: DBD = 'the brain is Dead, the Blood still flows'; DCD = 'the Circulation stopped'.

items.gloss_md: Deceased-donor livers in Eurotransplant are allocated mainly by urgency: high-urgency (HU) patients first, then elective patients by their match MELD (lab MELD or exceptional MELD), with blood group compatibility rules.
items.body_md:
- Introduced in Germany in December 2006 ('sickest first'), replacing waiting-time-based allocation.
- Match MELD = the higher of lab MELD and exceptional MELD (standard or non-standard exceptions, e.g. for HCC within Milan, PSC with cholangitis, HPS, PoPH, polycystic liver disease, familial amyloidosis).
- Lab MELD must be recertified at intervals that depend on its height (higher MELD, more frequent updates).
- HU status: acute liver failure (King's College or Clichy criteria), PNF or early hepatic artery thrombosis after transplant, acute Wilson disease and others.
- Paediatric patients receive priority. Split livers from suitable donors are used for a child and an adult.
- Rescue allocation (centre-oriented/competitive) applies to organs declined by several centres or with marginal quality. In Germany a substantial share of livers is placed this way.
- Allocation by 'sickest first' leads to sicker recipients and worse post-transplant outcomes, which is a continuing debate (survival benefit models).

attrs.mnemonic: Order of the liver queue: 'HU first, then MELD, blood group always'.

items.label_md: Liver transplant evaluation, indications and listing
items.gloss_md: The multidisciplinary process that decides whether a patient with liver disease should be placed on the waiting list. It weighs expected benefit (MELD, complications, tumour criteria) against contraindications (comorbidity, active substance use, extrahepatic cancer, poor support).
items.body_md:
- Typical triggers for evaluation: MELD ≥15, first decompensation (ascites, bleeding, HE), HCC within criteria, ALF (urgent), recurrent cholangitis in PSC, intractable pruritus, HPS, metabolic disease.
- Work-up: cardiopulmonary (echo, stress test, coronary angiography if needed), infection screening (HIV, HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV, TB), dental, cancer screening, psychosocial and addiction assessment, imaging (vessels, tumour), blood group and HLA (antibodies).
- Contraindications: uncontrolled sepsis, active extrahepatic malignancy, HCC beyond criteria with high AFP or extrahepatic spread, severe cardiopulmonary disease (including severe PoPH), ongoing substance abuse, lack of adherence.
- In Germany, the Bundesärztekammer guidelines (Richtlinien) under the Transplantationsgesetz define listing. A centre conference (interdisciplinary transplant conference) decides. For alcohol-associated cirrhosis, a period of abstinence (traditionally 6 months) and addiction-medicine assessment are required; the exact rules have been revised over time.

attrs.mnemonic: Listing logic: 'Sick enough to benefit (MELD ≥15 or decompensated), well enough to survive surgery, and able to look after the graft.'

items.gloss_md: MELD extended by serum sodium, because hyponatraemia independently predicts mortality in cirrhosis. It is used for US liver allocation from 2016 until MELD 3.0 in 2023.
items.body_md:
MELD-Na = MELD + 1.32 × (137 − Na) − [0.033 × MELD × (137 − Na)], with sodium bounded between 125 and 137 mmol/L.

- Applied only when MELD is above 11 (OPTN rule).
- Hyponatraemia reflects severe circulatory dysfunction (ADH activation) and is common with ascites and refractory ascites.
- Eurotransplant has long used the original lab MELD for allocation. Refitted versions (e.g. ReMELD-Na, developed with ET data) have been studied as successors. Check the current ET manual for the exact score in use.

attrs.mnemonic: Na below 137 adds points: 'Salt lost, points gained'.

items.gloss_md: Donation of a kidney or part of the liver (rarely lung lobe, pancreas segment or intestine) by a healthy living person. It provides the best graft quality and shortens waiting time, at a small but real risk to the donor.
items.body_md:
- Kidney: about a quarter to a third of kidney transplants in Germany. Donor work-up covers kidney function, blood pressure, glucose, anatomy and psychological assessment. Lifetime ESKD risk of the donor is slightly increased compared with matched healthy non-donors.
- Liver: living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT), right lobe for adults, left lateral segment for children.
- ABO-incompatible and HLA-incompatible living donation is possible with desensitisation. Kidney exchange ('Überkreuzspende', paired exchange) allows incompatible pairs to swap donors. In Germany, crossover donation has so far been possible only where a close personal relationship exists, which has blocked national kidney-exchange programmes; a reform has been under discussion.
- Germany: only between relatives or persons with a close personal relationship; subsidiary to deceased donation; approved by a Lebendspendekommission.

attrs.mnemonic: Living donation: 'best organ, shortest wait, healthy donor at risk'.

items.gloss_md: Organ donation after death is declared by circulatory criteria (cardiac arrest and a no-touch period), most often after planned withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (Maastricht III). It is practised in the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, the UK, Spain and the US, but not permitted in Germany.
items.body_md:
- Modified Maastricht categories: I found dead; II unsuccessful resuscitation (uncontrolled); III awaiting cardiac arrest after withdrawal of treatment (controlled, most common); IV cardiac arrest in a brain-dead donor; (V) in some versions, medically assisted death (euthanasia) in Belgium and the Netherlands.
- No-touch period after circulatory arrest: commonly 5 minutes (up to 20 minutes in Italy).
- Functional donor warm ischaemia (from significant hypotension/hypoxia to cold perfusion) damages especially bile ducts. DCD livers have more ischaemic cholangiopathy and PNF.
- Outcomes improved with normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) in the donor and machine perfusion (HOPE, NMP) after procurement.
- Germany imports DCD organs only indirectly. Introducing DCD is discussed politically.

attrs.mnemonic: Maastricht categories go from least to most controlled: I 'Found dead', II 'Failed CPR', III 'Await arrest' (controlled), IV 'Brain dead, then arrest'.
attrs.anecdote: The categories are named after an international workshop held in Maastricht in 1995.

items.label_md: Eurotransplant Kidney Allocation System (ETKAS) and ESP
items.gloss_md: Points-based kidney allocation in Eurotransplant (ETKAS) that weighs HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatches, waiting time on dialysis, mismatch probability, distance and country balance. ESP allocates kidneys from donors 65 years and older locally to recipients 65 and older without HLA matching.
items.body_md:
- ETKAS points: HLA mismatch points (most for 000-mismatch), waiting time from dialysis start, mismatch probability (rare HLA type or high sensitisation), distance (local cold ischaemia), national kidney exchange balance; bonus for children and for previous living donors.
- Full house (000 HLA-A/B/DR mismatch) kidneys receive priority.
- Acceptable Mismatch (AM) programme: highly sensitised patients (high vPRA) are offered kidneys from donors with HLA antigens their antibodies do not target ('acceptable' mismatches).
- Eurotransplant Senior Program (ESP, since 1999): old-for-old, local allocation to shorten cold ischaemia time, which matters more than HLA for old kidneys.

attrs.mnemonic: ETKAS counts 'HLA, time and rarity'; ESP says 'old to old, keep it cold (short)'.

items.gloss_md: Updated MELD (Kim et al., 2021) that adds female sex and albumin to bilirubin, INR, creatinine and sodium (with interaction terms and creatinine capped at 3.0 mg/dL). It was introduced for US liver allocation in July 2023.
items.body_md:
- Variables: sex (female +1.33), bilirubin, sodium, INR, creatinine, albumin. Interactions: bilirubin × sodium, albumin × creatinine.
- Corrects the disadvantage of women (lower muscle mass means lower creatinine for the same kidney function, which underestimated their MELD) and improves discrimination.
- Lower creatinine cap (3.0 instead of 4.0).
- MELD 3.0 is the current OPTN (US) allocation score. Eurotransplant has evaluated similar updates.

attrs.mnemonic: 3.0 = 3 new things: sex, albumin, and a cap at 3.0.

items.label_md: Brain death (irreversible loss of brain function)
items.gloss_md: Irreversible cessation of all functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem with preserved circulation on ventilation. In Germany it is the legal prerequisite for deceased organ donation (DBD).
items.body_md:
- German term: 'irreversibler Hirnfunktionsausfall' (IHA) per Bundesärztekammer guideline (fourth update 2015, with later revisions).
- Diagnosis in three steps: (1) prerequisites (known severe primary or secondary brain injury, exclusion of reversible causes such as intoxication, sedation, hypothermia, metabolic disturbances); (2) clinical signs (coma, loss of brainstem reflexes, apnoea test); (3) proof of irreversibility (observation period or ancillary tests such as EEG, evoked potentials, perfusion scintigraphy, CT angiography, transcranial Doppler).
- Determined independently by two qualified physicians not involved in transplantation.
- Brain death triggers a catecholamine storm, diabetes insipidus and systemic inflammation, which affect organ quality and require intensive donor management.

attrs.anecdote: The concept of brain death was formalised by the Harvard Ad Hoc Committee in 1968 ('irreversible coma'), one year after the first heart transplant.

items.gloss_md: The highest priority status on the Eurotransplant waiting list for patients who will die within days without a transplant, e.g. acute liver failure, primary non-function or early hepatic artery thrombosis.
items.body_md:
- Liver HU criteria: ALF meeting King's College or Clichy criteria; PNF or hepatic artery thrombosis within 14 days of transplant; acute Wilson disease or Budd–Chiari with failure; anhepatic state; severe trauma.
- Reviewed by Eurotransplant auditors and recertified after a short interval (days).
- Heart: HU for patients on inotropes or with mechanical support complications. Kidney: HU for patients who cannot be dialysed (no vascular access).

attrs.mnemonic: HU = 'Hours Until' — days to live without an organ.

items.gloss_md: Transplantation of part of a living donor's liver: right lobe (segments V–VIII) for adults, left lobe or left lateral segment (II–III) for children. Both donor liver and graft regenerate within weeks.
items.body_md:
- Graft-to-recipient weight ratio (GRWR) should be at least about 0.8% (or graft volume ≥40% of the recipient's standard liver volume) to avoid small-for-size syndrome (cholestasis, ascites, coagulopathy from portal hyperperfusion).
- Donor: remnant liver volume ≥30–35%, no relevant steatosis. Donor complications in a substantial minority. Donor mortality is low but not zero.
- Dominant in Asia (Japan, Korea), where deceased donation is rare. In Germany LDLT is a small share of liver transplants.
- Advantages: planned timing, short ischaemia, transplantation before deterioration.

attrs.mnemonic: '0.8 is great': GRWR ≥0.8% avoids small-for-size.

items.gloss_md: Extra MELD points assigned to patients whose risk of dying or of losing transplant eligibility is not captured by lab MELD. The most common reason is HCC within the Milan criteria.
items.body_md:
- Standard exceptions (SE) in Eurotransplant/Germany include: HCC within Milan (in cirrhosis, with tumour ≥2 cm or multiple lesions), hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, PSC with recurrent cholangitis, polycystic liver disease, familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy, primary hyperoxaluria, cystic fibrosis, urea cycle defects, small-for-size syndrome after partial LT, hepatoblastoma, hilar cholangiocarcinoma in some protocols.
- Exceptional MELD starts at a value corresponding to a defined 3-month mortality and increases every 3 months while the criteria still apply.
- Non-standard exceptions (NSE) are decided by an expert audit group.
- Exception points can disadvantage patients with high lab MELD. The US uses the median MELD at transplant minus 3 (MMaT-3) for HCC to address this.

attrs.mnemonic: Exception points speak for risks lab values cannot see: the tumour (HCC) cannot raise bilirubin, but it can grow beyond Milan.

items.gloss_md: German federal law of 1997 that regulates organ donation, procurement, allocation and transplantation. It requires brain death (irreversible loss of all brain function) for deceased donation and restricts living donation to close relatives or persons with a close personal relationship.
items.body_md:
- Deceased donation only after irreversible loss of whole-brain function (Hirntod), diagnosed by two qualified physicians according to Bundesärztekammer guidelines. Donation after circulatory death (DCD) is therefore not permitted in Germany.
- Consent: 'Entscheidungslösung' (decision solution, since 2012). Citizens are regularly asked to document their decision. Without a documented decision, relatives decide according to the presumed wishes. An opt-out ('Widerspruchslösung') was rejected by the Bundestag in January 2020 and remains under debate.
- Online organ donor register (Organspende-Register) since March 2024.
- Living donation (§8): only kidney and part of the liver (and a few others); donor must be an adult and a relative or close person; subsidiarity (only if no deceased organ is available); independent living donation commission (Lebendspendekommission).
- After the 2012 allocation manipulation scandal (falsified lab data in several liver programmes), oversight was tightened: audit commissions, the 'six-eye principle' for listing, criminal penalties.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) TPG in drei Worten: 'Hirntod, Entscheidung, Nähe' — brain death for deceased donors, a documented decision (Entscheidungslösung), and living donation only between close persons.
attrs.anecdote: In 2012 it emerged that doctors in Göttingen and other centres had falsified lab values (e.g. claimed dialysis) to raise their patients' MELD scores. The scandal caused donation numbers in Germany to drop sharply in the following years.

items.gloss_md: Division of one deceased-donor liver into two grafts: typically a left lateral segment (II–III) for a child and an extended right graft (I, IV–VIII) for an adult, or two hemilivers for two adults.
items.body_md:
- Increases the number of grafts and is essential for paediatric transplantation (small children need small grafts).
- Done in situ (in the donor) or ex situ (on the back table).
- Requires an excellent donor (young, short ICU stay, no steatosis). Eurotransplant rules require suitable livers to be offered for splitting.
- Slightly higher biliary and vascular complication rates than whole grafts.

attrs.mnemonic: 'One donor, two lives': left lateral (II–III) for the child, the rest for the adult.
attrs.anecdote: The first split-liver transplantation was performed by Rudolf Pichlmayr at the Medizinische Hochschule Hannover in 1988.

items.gloss_md: The national coordinating body for post-mortem organ donation in Germany. It supports hospitals in identifying donors, organises donor management and organ procurement, and reports donor organs to Eurotransplant.
items.body_md:
- Commissioned under the Transplantationsgesetz. Seven regions with coordinators.
- Every hospital with an intensive care unit (Entnahmekrankenhaus) must appoint a transplant officer (Transplantationsbeauftragter), strengthened by the 2019 law.
- Publishes the annual donation statistics: around 950–1000 deceased donors per year (about 11 per million inhabitants), much lower than Spain (over 45 pmp).
- Organ allocation itself is done by Eurotransplant, according to rules from the Bundesärztekammer.

attrs.mnemonic: Three players in Germany: DSO procures, Eurotransplant allocates, the transplant centre transplants (and the BÄK writes the rules).

items.gloss_md: Tissue damage that develops when blood flow returns to an organ after ischaemia. Reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial dysfunction, sterile inflammation and microcirculatory failure follow, causing graft dysfunction, rejection risk and biliary injury.
items.body_md:
- During ischaemia, ATP falls and succinate accumulates. On reperfusion, rapid succinate oxidation through mitochondrial complex II drives reverse electron transport at complex I and a burst of ROS (Chouchani et al., Nature 2014).
- Cascade: DAMPs (HMGB1, mtDNA) activate TLRs on Kupffer cells, followed by cytokines (TNF, IL-1), complement, neutrophil influx, endothelial injury and no-reflow, then hepatocyte and cholangiocyte death.
- Clinical consequences: post-reperfusion syndrome, EAD/PNF, DGF in kidneys, primary graft dysfunction in lungs, ischaemic cholangiopathy. Inflammation increases immunogenicity (alloimmune activation).
- Mitigation: short ischaemia times, hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (reloads mitochondria and reduces ROS on reperfusion), NMP, ischaemic preconditioning, drugs in trials.
- A frequent topic of transcriptomic and metabolomic studies of pre- and post-reperfusion biopsies.

attrs.mnemonic: 'The damage comes with the oxygen': ischaemia sets up the bomb (succinate), reperfusion lights the fuse (ROS burst).

items.gloss_md: Preservation of donor organs by continuous perfusion with a device instead of static cold storage, either hypothermic (HMP/HOPE) or normothermic (NMP). It improves outcomes, extends preservation and allows viability testing before transplantation.
items.body_md:
- Hypothermic (4–12 °C): HMP for kidneys (standard in Eurotransplant for many kidneys), HOPE/D-HOPE for livers (oxygenated, usually 1–2 h at the end of cold storage).
- Normothermic (35–37 °C): NMP with oxygenated blood-based perfusate, keeps the organ metabolically active. Liver (OrganOx metra), heart (TransMedics OCS), lung (EVLP).
- Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP): ECMO-like perfusion in the DCD donor before procurement.
- Benefits shown in RCTs: fewer biliary complications (HOPE in DCD livers), lower discard, longer safe preservation (NMP), better early function of kidneys (oxygenated HMP).
- Perfusate and bile analysis offers a 'liquid biopsy' of graft quality (lactate, pH, glucose, ALT, FMN, cfDNA, omics).

attrs.mnemonic: 'Cold machine repairs, warm machine tests': HOPE recharges mitochondria, NMP lets you watch the organ work.

items.gloss_md: Time from the cold perfusion of the organ in the donor until it is taken out of cold storage for implantation (or reperfused). Longer CIT increases graft dysfunction.
items.body_md:
- Cooling to about 4 °C lowers metabolism about 10–12-fold but does not stop it: ATP is depleted, and succinate and other metabolites accumulate, which drives ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
- Approximate tolerance: heart ideally below 4 h; lung 6–8 h; liver ideally below 8–12 h; pancreas below 12 h; kidney up to about 24 h (each extra hour raises the risk of delayed graft function).
- In Germany CIT is a frequent quality concern because organs are often transported far through Eurotransplant.
- Machine perfusion extends safe preservation and allows organ assessment.

attrs.mnemonic: Tolerance ranking 'Heart 4, Lung 6, Liver 12, Kidney 24' — roughly doubling as you go down the list.

items.gloss_md: Need for dialysis within the first week after kidney transplantation. It reflects acute tubular injury, mostly from ischaemia-reperfusion, and is associated with worse long-term graft outcomes and more rejection.
items.body_md:
- Incidence: roughly 20–30% of deceased-donor kidneys in Europe, higher (up to about half) in DCD; rare in living donation.
- Risk factors: long CIT, DCD, donor age and AKI, recipient factors (obesity, re-transplant, sensitisation).
- Reduced by hypothermic machine perfusion and short CIT.
- Requires closer monitoring because rejection can be masked. Biopsy if no recovery after about 7–10 days.

attrs.mnemonic: DGF = 'Dialysis in the first week'.

items.gloss_md: End-ischaemic perfusion of the donor liver (or kidney) at about 8–12 °C with a highly oxygenated acellular solution, usually for 1–2 hours before implantation. It reloads mitochondria and reduces reperfusion injury and biliary complications.
items.body_md:
- HOPE perfuses the portal vein only. D-HOPE (dual) perfuses portal vein and hepatic artery.
- Mechanism: under cold, oxygenated conditions, the accumulated succinate is metabolised and ATP is restored without the ROS burst. Mitochondrial flavin mononucleotide (FMN) released into the perfusate is a damage marker that predicts graft function.
- Evidence: DHOPE-DCD trial (van Rijn et al., NEJM 2021): fewer symptomatic non-anastomotic biliary strictures in DCD livers. HOPE-ECD-DBD trial (Czigany et al., Ann Surg 2021, Aachen): fewer complications with extended-criteria DBD livers. Further trials confirmed reduced complications.
- Simple, transportable devices (e.g. Liver Assist, VitaSmart). Widely adopted in Europe, including German centres.

attrs.mnemonic: HOPE gives the liver 'hope' in the cold: oxygen in, succinate out, before warm blood returns.
attrs.anecdote: HOPE was developed largely in Zurich by Philipp Dutkowski and Pierre-Alain Clavien. They showed that a short oxygenated cold perfusion at the end of storage was enough to protect DCD livers.

items.gloss_md: Perfusion of the donor organ at body temperature with an oxygenated, usually red-cell-based perfusate and nutrients. The organ stays metabolically active, which allows long preservation and functional testing before transplantation.
items.body_md:
- Liver NMP (e.g. OrganOx metra, Liver Assist in normothermic mode): COPE trial (Nasralla et al., Nature 2018) showed 50% less graft injury (peak AST), 50% lower discard rate and 54% longer preservation versus static cold storage.
- Viability criteria (e.g. UK VITTAL trial): lactate clearance, perfusate pH, bile production and bile pH/glucose, stable flows. Allows transplantation of initially declined livers.
- Can preserve livers for more than 24 hours, opening possibilities for ex vivo repair (defatting, drug or gene therapy).
- Heart: TransMedics OCS (beating heart). Lung: EVLP (Toronto, Cypel et al., NEJM 2011). Kidney: short NMP (Cambridge/Nicholson).

attrs.mnemonic: NMP = 'Normal temperature, Measure Performance': the organ works on the machine so you can test it.

items.gloss_md: Initially poor function of a liver graft that eventually recovers. By the Olthoff criteria it is defined as bilirubin ≥10 mg/dL or INR ≥1.6 on day 7, or AST/ALT above 2000 IU/L within the first 7 days.
items.body_md:
- Olthoff et al. (Liver Transplantation 2010). Occurs in about a quarter of liver transplants and is associated with higher graft loss and mortality.
- Causes: donor quality (age, steatosis, DCD), long CIT, ischaemia-reperfusion injury, small-for-size grafts, technical problems.
- Continuous risk models: MEAF, L-GrAFT.
- EAD is a common endpoint in machine perfusion trials and in biomarker or omics studies of graft quality.

attrs.mnemonic: Olthoff: '10 – 1.6 – 2000' = bilirubin 10, INR 1.6 on day 7, transaminases 2000 in week 1.

items.gloss_md: Irreversible failure of a transplanted organ to ever function, without a technical (vascular) cause. For the liver it is a life-threatening emergency that requires urgent re-transplantation.
items.body_md:
- Liver PNF: severe acidosis, rising lactate, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, very high transaminases, encephalopathy, renal failure, no bile production, in the first days after transplantation. Hepatic artery thrombosis must be excluded.
- Incidence a few percent. Risk factors: donor quality (DCD, steatosis, age), long CIT, severe ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
- In Eurotransplant, PNF within 14 days qualifies for high-urgency re-listing.
- Kidney PNF: the graft never starts working and the patient stays on dialysis (distinguish from delayed graft function, which recovers).

attrs.mnemonic: PNF = 'Never Functioned' (and won't); EAD = 'Early, but Recovers'.

items.gloss_md: Donor whose organs carry a higher risk of graft dysfunction or failure (e.g. older age, steatosis, long ischaemia, DCD, high sodium), but which are increasingly used because of the organ shortage.
items.body_md:
- Liver: donor age over 65, macrovesicular steatosis over 40% (or over 30%), ICU stay over 7 days, BMI over 30, sodium over 165 mmol/L, raised transaminases, cold ischaemia over 12 h, DCD (Eurotransplant/BÄK criteria vary).
- Kidney (UNOS definition): any donor ≥60, or 50–59 with two of hypertension, creatinine >1.5 mg/dL, or death from stroke. Now replaced in the US by the continuous KDPI.
- Scores: Donor Risk Index (DRI), Eurotransplant-DRI, KDRI/KDPI (kidney).
- Machine perfusion is used to assess and improve ECD organs.
- Germany has an old donor pool (median donor age well above 50), so a large share of organs are ECD.

items.gloss_md: Time an organ spends without perfusion at body or room temperature. Donor warm ischaemia occurs in DCD before cold flush, and recipient (implantation) warm ischaemia occurs during the anastomoses. It is much more damaging per minute than cold ischaemia.
items.body_md:
- Donor (functional) WIT in DCD: from significant hypotension/hypoxia (e.g. systolic BP <50 mmHg or SpO₂ <70%) after withdrawal of treatment to cold perfusion. Livers usually tolerate up to about 20–30 min, kidneys longer.
- Recipient WIT (anastomosis time): typically 30–60 min for liver or kidney. Longer times are associated with DGF and EAD.
- Damage: rapid ATP loss, mitochondrial injury, microcirculatory failure. In the liver, mainly ischaemic cholangiopathy.

attrs.mnemonic: Warm minutes are like cold hours: a few minutes warm hurt as much as hours on ice.

items.gloss_md: Thrombotic occlusion of the hepatic artery anastomosis after liver transplantation. Because bile ducts depend on arterial blood, it causes biliary necrosis, abscesses and graft failure.
items.body_md:
- Early HAT (within about 30 days) occurs in a few percent of adults, more in children and LDLT. Early HAT can cause fulminant graft failure and qualifies for HU re-listing (within 14 days in ET).
- Routine Doppler ultrasound surveillance in the first days after LT. Confirmation by CT angiography.
- Treatment: urgent revascularisation (thrombectomy/re-anastomosis, interventional thrombolysis/stenting) or re-transplantation.
- Late HAT may present as ischaemic biliary strictures, bilomas or cholangitis.

attrs.mnemonic: 'No artery, no bile ducts': in the transplanted liver the artery alone feeds the bile ducts.

items.gloss_md: Diffuse strictures and casts of the intrahepatic bile ducts after liver transplantation, caused by ischaemic injury of the biliary epithelium and peribiliary plexus. It is a typical complication of DCD grafts and a major cause of re-transplantation.
items.body_md:
- Also called ischaemic-type biliary lesions (ITBL) or non-anastomotic strictures (NAS), as opposed to anastomotic strictures (technical, treated well by ERCP).
- Risk factors: DCD (donor warm ischaemia), long CIT, older donors, hepatic artery problems, immunological injury.
- Presents weeks to months after LT with cholestasis and cholangitis. MRCP/ERCP show irregular strictures.
- Machine perfusion (HOPE, NRP) markedly reduces its incidence.
